lessons.title: Wondering About Science

activities.prompt: What can you discover when you stay curious?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Wondering About Science
activities.body:
Imagine science as a big adventure. You begin by asking questions and exploring the world around you. As you think, observe and do things, science helps you understand what you see. Your curiosity is the most important quality for science.

Now, notice a tiny grain of sand. Then turn your eyes towards a huge mountain. Science can explore both, from the tiniest details to the greatest heights. Each view can open fresh questions in your mind.

Next, lift your gaze to the night sky. Its stars may make you wonder why they shine. New questions can appear, and science gives you ways to explore them. Curiosity helps you keep asking, looking and understanding.

Perhaps you also watch a flower. You may wonder how it knows when to open. Such questions show why curiosity matters so much. As you ask, observe and explore, nature always offers something new and exciting to discover.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What is science?
activities.body: Science helps us understand the world by thinking, observing and doing things. It is a big adventure where we ask questions and explore. Curiosity means wanting to ask questions and find out more. It is the most important quality for science. We can explore tiny grains of sand and huge mountains. The night sky may make us wonder why stars shine.
keyPoints: Science helps us understand the world.
Curiosity helps us ask questions and explore.
Science can explore tiny things and huge things.
activities.explanation: Curiosity helps you begin every science adventure.

We look closely at the flower. Looking helps us understand the world around us.
We think about what we notice. Science grows through questions and exploring.
So we keep our curiosity and keep exploring. Curiosity is the most important quality for science.

lessons.title: Science Is Everywhere

activities.prompt: Where might your next science discovery begin?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Science Is Everywhere
activities.body:
Imagine you begin your science tour in the kitchen. You might ask what your food is made of. Science can help you find out. Next, you travel to outer space, where science can be studied.

Your tour then takes you to the playground. Science discoveries can begin here. Many groundbreaking discoveries have come from places we do not expect.

Now picture science as a huge jigsaw puzzle that never ends. Each new discovery adds another piece. New knowledge leads to more questions and more things to find out. You see how one discovery can lead to the next.

New discoveries can change how we understand the world. A discovery may show that an old idea was in the wrong place. You picture yourself moving a puzzle piece. Your new understanding helps you ask fresh questions.

Finally, your tour brings you home to Earth. It is our home and the only planet we know that supports life. Earth has many kinds of plants and animals. They survive in different regions. We must protect the environment of our planet.

lessons.title: Water, Materials and Scientific Questions

activities.prompt: How does water change when it gets very cold or very hot?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Water and Material Mysteries
activities.body:
You begin with a rainy-day puddle. It makes you curious about rain. You can ask why and how it rains. You also know that you need both food and water to survive.

Now you explore water and its changes. It freezes into ice when it is cooled. It boils and becomes steam when it is heated. You may enjoy cool water in summer and warm water in winter.

These changes lead you to another question. How can we tell how hot something is? Understanding hot and cold helps us know this. Measuring temperature is important during a fever.

Next, you look around your home. Many everyday objects are made from different materials. You wonder whether different objects use different materials. Science helps you work out how to separate them.

Finally, you think about science. Science is not only about memorising facts and figures. It helps you ask questions and find answers. You can keep asking questions and seeking answers.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Water, heat and materials
activities.body: We need food and water to survive. A puddle can make us curious about rain. We can ask why and how it rains. Water becomes ice when cooled and steam when heated. Hot and cold show how hot things are. Measuring how hot something is matters during a fever. Materials are the things used to make objects. Science helps separate materials. Science is not only about memorising facts and figures.
keyPoints: Food and water help us survive.
Cooling and heating change water.
Science helps us ask questions and separate materials.
activities.explanation: These ideas show how questions help us understand water, materials and science.

lessons.title: Finding Answers with Guesses and Tests

activities.prompt: How can you find out why your pen stops writing?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Pen Problem
activities.body:
You might not notice when you are finding an answer. Finding answers is something you have already been doing. You use this skill whenever you wonder what has happened.

Now imagine that your pen stops writing. You have a problem to investigate. First, you ask yourself why the pen has stopped writing. One possible answer is that the ink has finished.

Next, you open the pen to check whether the ink has finished. If you find an empty ink refill, your guess was correct. The empty refill gives you the answer you needed.

However, if the ink is not finished, you need another possible answer. You might guess that the ink has dried up. You test this new guess by trying something else.

The pen problem shows you how science works. You ask, make a guess, and then test it. A test helps you find out whether your answer is right.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How We Find Answers
activities.body: We often find answers without noticing it. A pen has stopped writing. This is a problem to solve. First, ask why it stopped writing. One possible answer is that the ink has run out. Open the pen to check. An empty refill tells us our guess was right. If not, try another answer. The ink might have dried up. Test this new guess.
keyPoints: We often find answers without noticing.
We ask why a problem has happened.
We check a guess and try another if needed.
activities.explanation: Nice work! The pen shows how guessing, checking and trying again help us find answers.

activities.prompt: What could be wrong with a pen that has stopped writing?
steps: A pen stops writing, which gives us a problem to investigate.
We ask why and make a possible answer: the ink has finished.
We open the pen because that checks the guess, and an empty refill tells us it was right.
If the ink is not finished, we guess it might have dried up and test this new guess, showing how science works.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: We often find answers without noticing that we are doing so.
activities.explanation: Yes! Finding answers is something we have already been doing, often without noticing.

Which pen should we buy?
How should we clean the pen?

activities.explanation: Good choice! We first ask why the pen has stopped writing.

activities.prompt: Match each clue with the right step in the pen test.
pairs: Why did the pen stop writing?
activities.explanation: Good! Each clue matches a step in the pen test.

activities.prompt: An empty ink refill tells us that our guess was ______.
activities.hint: Open the pen and check the refill.
activities.explanation: Exactly! An empty ink refill tells us that our guess was correct.

activities.prompt: The ink is not finished. What should we do next?
options: Keep the first guess and stop checking.
Choose an answer without testing it.
Stop investigating the pen.
Try another possible answer and test it.
activities.explanation: Well done! If the ink is not finished, we need another possible answer.

activities.prompt: An empty ink refill shows that the dried-up guess was correct.
activities.explanation: Good check! The empty refill supports the guess that the ink has finished.

activities.prompt: Put the pen investigation steps in the correct order.
items: Ask why the pen stopped writing
Guess that the ink has finished
Open the pen to check

activities.explanation: Excellent! The steps move from a question to guesses, checks, and another test.

activities.prompt: Why does the pen problem show how science works?
options: It replaces checking with guessing.
It always accepts the first possible answer.
It checks a guess and tries again when needed.
It finds answers without noticing a problem.
activities.explanation: Great thinking! The problem uses a guess, a check, and another tested guess.

activities.prompt: A pen stops writing while a child is doing homework. The child opens it and sees that the ink refill is empty. What should the child conclude?
options: The ink has now finished.
The ink might have dried up.
The pen needs another test.

Drying up is a different guess, not the one this check confirms.
The empty refill has already checked the correct guess.
A stopped pen shows a problem, not that the pen is working well.

activities.explanation: An empty refill shows that the ink-finished guess was right.

activities.prompt: Which sequence best shows how science works in the pen problem?
options: Ask, guess, test, then guess again.
Test first, then make no guess.
Make one guess and never check it.
Ask, but do not test the answer.

The pen investigation begins with asking why before making a possible answer.
One untested guess would not show how the pen problem is investigated.
Asking why without testing the answer leaves the guess unchecked.

activities.explanation: The method starts by asking why, making a guess, and testing it.

lessons.title: The Scientific Method

activities.prompt: What could you discover on a little science adventure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Scientific Method Tour
activities.body:
You notice something interesting or puzzling. Observation makes you wonder and think of a question. You turn that wonder into a clear question. Your curiosity begins the scientific method.

Next, you guess a possible answer. You test that guess through experiments or further observations. Testing comes after your guess.

The scientific method helps you work through a problem. Scientists follow it to solve problems and discover new things. Anyone who follows it works like a scientist.

Ordinary life can include this method too. A cook may use it while wondering why dal has spilled. A bicycle repairer may look for the reason that a tyre is flat.

You can use the method in science and in everyday life. It helps people solve problems or find new things. When you follow its steps, you work like a scientist.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How scientists solve problems
activities.body: Scientists solve problems in steps. First, you notice something. It is interesting or puzzling. This makes you wonder. You think of a question. Then you make the question clear. You guess a possible answer. Next, you test your guess. Use experiments or more observations. This helps people solve problems. It also helps them find new things.
keyPoints: Noticing something makes us wonder and ask a question.
We make the question clear. We guess a possible answer.
We test the guess with experiments or more observations.
activities.explanation: Scientists turn wonder into clear questions and tested guesses.

activities.prompt: Why is a bicycle tyre flat?
steps: A bicycle repairer sees a flat tyre, and this observation begins the scientific method because it is something puzzling.
The observation makes the repairer wonder, so the wonder is turned into a clear question: why is the tyre flat?
A possible answer is guessed because this is the next step after forming a clear question.
The guess is tested through an experiment or further observation because a guess needs checking, so the repairer follows the method to investigate the flat tyre.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

lessons.title: A Scientific Journey Together

activities.prompt: What could we discover if we started our science journey together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey of Wonder
activities.body:
You begin your science journey with a simple wonder. Something around you catches your attention. You pause and observe your surroundings carefully. Curiosity leads you to ask how and why questions.

Curiosity is the first and foremost quality for learning science. You use the scientific method in daily-life situations. You apply it to some extent, just as all of us do. Your learning journey starts with this useful habit.

Learning science develops your ability to find solutions. Your questions lead you towards many unknown things waiting for you to explore. You keep observing carefully. Curiosity keeps guiding your learning.

Science helps you solve bigger problems and mysteries of the universe. Scientific work is rarely done by one person alone. Scientists often work together in large teams. Perhaps your classmates join your exploration.

Together, you share the work of exploration. Science should be a joyful journey of exploration. You keep asking how and why. Many unknown things wait for your curiosity.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Science Is a Shared Journey
activities.body: We often use the scientific method in daily life. We all use it a little. Curiosity is the most important quality for learning science. Curiosity means wanting to know things. It helps us ask how and why questions. We should observe (watch carefully) our surroundings. We should explore the many things we do not know. Scientists rarely work alone. So teamwork matters. Science helps us find solutions and solve big problems. It also helps us explore the mysteries of the universe. Science should be a joyful journey.
keyPoints: Use the scientific method in daily life.

lessons.title: Seeing Diversity Around Us

activities.prompt: What wonders might you discover on a quiet nature walk?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Walk Full of Life
activities.body:
You begin your nature walk by looking closely at what lives nearby. You see grasses, bushes and large trees. The walk helps you experience the beauty and variety of plants and animals. You observe living creatures without disturbing them.

Listen carefully, and each bird offers its own unique chirp. Look at leaves, too. Their shapes differ. Their arrangements on stems or branches also differ.

Stop beside flowers and compare their colours, shapes and scents. Notice how flowers can look or smell different from each other. Now watch where animals live. Some stay on land, while others live in trees. Frogs can live both on land and in water. You see animals living in different places.

As the walk continues, you notice the variety of plants and animals around you. This variety forms part of the region's biodiversity. You see that plants and animals depend on one another. The walk has helped you experience nature's beauty and variety.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Many Kinds of Nature
activities.body: A nature walk helps you see many plants and animals. Watch them, but do not bother them. You can see grass, bushes and big trees. Each bird sings in its own way. Leaves and flowers look different. Frogs can live on land and in water. The variety of life in a place is called biodiversity. Plants and animals need each other.
keyPoints: Watch living things without bothering them.
Leaves and flowers look different.
Plants and animals need each other.
activities.explanation: Nature has many differences. We should always be kind to living things.

activities.prompt: During a nature walk, a student sees grasses, bushes, large trees, flowers, birds, and a frog. What should the student notice, and how should the student behave?
steps: The student should notice the grasses, bushes, and large trees because the walk shows that plant life is not all alike.
The student should compare the leaves and flowers because leaves differ in shape and arrangement, while flowers differ in colour, shape, and scent.

The student should watch the animals quietly and note where they live because some live on land, some live in trees, and frogs can live in both land and water, while all living creatures should not be disturbed.
The varied plant and animal life is part of the region's biodiversity, and the student should remember that plants and animals depend on one another.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

Watch it without bothering it
Pick it up for a short time
Make noise next to it
activities.explanation: Living things should be watched without bothering them.

activities.hint: Think about both places where a frog can live.
activities.explanation: Frogs can live both on land and in water.

activities.prompt: Match each living thing with its feature or home.

Living on land and in water

Bushes

Chirp
Arrangement
Biodiversity

activities.prompt: A frog moves from the edge of a pond onto wet ground. Which guess makes sense?
options: It can live in both places, because frogs live on land and in water.
It can live only in the pond, because frogs must always swim.
It can live only on land, because frogs cannot stay in water.
It cannot live in either place, because frogs must live in trees.

why.It can live only in the pond, because fr: This answer is wrong. It thinks a frog must always be in water.
why.It can live only on land, because frogs: This answer is wrong. It thinks a frog cannot go into water.

activities.prompt: A student wants to compare how the leaves are arranged on two branches. What is the best way?

Pick one leaf from each branch and hide the stems.
Count only the flowers on both branches. Ignore the leaves.
Touch the leaves so their shapes and places are clearer.

why.Pick one leaf from each branch and hide: This is wrong. One leaf cannot show how all the leaves are arranged.
This is wrong. Flowers are not leaves.
why.Touch the leaves so their shapes and pla: This is wrong. Touching the plant does not help us observe it.

activities.explanation: This is right. Leaves can be different in shape and in arrangement on stems or branches.

activities.prompt: Two flowers look alike at first. Which observation best checks how they differ?

Compare only their colours because colour shows every difference.
Compare only their shapes because flowers never vary in scent.
Compare their scents alone because flowers do not vary in shape.

why.Compare only their shapes because flower: This mistake comes from thinking shape is the only feature that can differ.
why.Compare their scents alone because flowe: This mistake comes from thinking scent is the only feature that can differ.

activities.explanation: This is right because flowers can differ in colour, shape, and scent.

Every bird on the ground makes a silent call.

why.Only the bird in the tree can make a chi: This mistake comes from assuming that only tree-dwelling birds can chirp.
why.Every bird on the ground makes a silent: This mistake comes from assuming that birds on the ground never chirp.

lessons.title: Grouping Plants and Animals

activities.prompt: What can we learn by grouping the plants and animals around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Grouping Plants and Animals
activities.body:
You begin a gentle tour of the plant and animal groups around you. Why are living things placed in different groups? We will look at the features that guide these groupings.

Plants can be grouped by height. Plant stems vary in thickness, height and hardness. You may see trees, which are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems. Flowers also guide grouping. Their presence or absence helps you sort plants.

Shrubs have hard woody stems that branch close to the ground. Herbs are usually small plants with soft and green stems. Climbers have weak stems and need support to climb and grow. Creepers grow along the ground.

Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement. As you look around, ask what an animal eats. Notice where it stays. Check its colour. Watch its movement.

Grouping makes plants and animals easier to understand and study. By noticing similarities and differences, you can compare each group. Sorting plants and animals gives you a clearer way to learn about them.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Different Features Make Groups
activities.body: We can group plants and animals by similarities and differences. Different groups may use different features. Plants can be grouped by height. They can also be grouped by whether they have flowers. Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement. Grouping helps people study plants and animals more easily.
keyPoints: Groups can use similarities and differences.
Plants may be grouped by height or flowers.
Animals may be grouped by food, place, colour and movement.
activities.explanation: Different features help us make useful groups.

activities.prompt: Three plants are mixed together. One is tall. Its stem is hard, thick, brown and woody. One has weak stems. It needs support. One grows along the ground. How should you group them?
steps: Group the plants by their stems and how they grow. Different groups may look at different parts.
Put the tall plant with trees. It has a hard, thick, brown, woody stem like a tree.
Put the plant with weak stems with climbers. Weak stems need support to climb.
Put the plant that grows on the ground with creepers. This makes the groups clear and easy to study.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Plant Groups and Their Stems
activities.body: Plant stems vary in thickness, height and hardness. Trees are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems. Shrubs have hard woody stems that branch close to the ground. Herbs are usually small plants with soft and green stems. Climbers have weak stems and need support. Creepers grow along the ground.
keyPoints: Trees have hard, thick, brown and woody stems.
Herbs are usually small with soft and green stems.
Climbers need support, while creepers grow along the ground.
activities.explanation: Stem and growth features help us recognise plant groups.

activities.prompt: Which feature can be used to group plants?
options: Height
Food
Movement

activities.explanation: Trees are tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems.

activities.explanation: These are all features used for grouping animals.

activities.prompt: Match each plant group with its correct feature.
pairs: Tall plants with hard, thick, brown and woody stems
Hard woody stems that branch close to the ground
Usually small plants with soft and green stems
Weak stems that need support to climb and grow

activities.prompt: Put these steps in the right order.
items: Pick features to group by
Group things by what is alike and what is different

activities.explanation: Features can help us group things. Groups make study easier.

activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a plant group with its stem feature?
options: Climbers — weak stems needing support
Trees — soft green stems
Herbs — stems branching close to the ground
Creepers — hard, thick, brown stems
activities.explanation: Climbers have weak stems and need support to climb and grow.

activities.prompt: One plant has a tall, hard, thick, brown stem. Another plant has a small, soft, green stem. Why are they in different groups?
options: Their stems differ in height, thickness, hardness and colour.
Their stems are the same, so the groups must match.
Only flowers can tell these two plants apart.
Their heights match, so stem features do not matter.

why.Their stems are the same, so the groups: This wrongly says both plants have the same stems.
why.Only flowers can tell these two plants a: This wrongly says only flowers can tell them apart.
why.Their heights match, so stem features do: This wrongly says matching height makes stems useless.

activities.explanation: The two plants have very different stems.

activities.prompt: A weak-stemmed plant is placed near a support so it can reach upward. What is the likely result, and why?
options: It climbs the support, because it needs support.
It creeps along the ground, because weak stems stay low.
It grows a thick woody stem, because support makes stems hard.
It stays the same height, because weak stems cannot grow.

why.It creeps along the ground, because weak: This mistake confuses a climber with a creeper.
why.It grows a thick woody stem, because sup: This mistake assumes support can make a weak stem hard and woody.
why.It stays the same height, because weak s: This mistake assumes a weak stem cannot grow at all.

activities.explanation: This is right because weak stems need support to climb and grow.

activities.prompt: Two plants are the same height. One has flowers. One has no flowers. A child says, 'They must be in the same group.' Is this fair?
options: No; their flowers can set them apart.
Yes; same height decides every group.
No; every plant group needs different heights.
Yes; flowers never matter for groups.

This mistake thinks height is the only rule for grouping.
why.No; every plant group needs different he: This mistake thinks every group must differ in every way.
This mistake believes flowers are never useful.

activities.explanation: This is right because flowers can group plants, even if they are the same height.

activities.prompt: One class groups animals by what they eat. Another groups them by where they live. Why can both plans be reasonable?
options: Animal groups may use different useful features.
Only one feature may be used for animal groups.
Food cannot be used when place is also used.
Both classes must group animals by movement.

why.Only one feature may be used for animal: This mistake assumes all animal groups must use one feature.
why.Food cannot be used when place is also u: This mistake thinks two different features cannot both be used.
why.Both classes must group animals by movem: This mistake assumes movement is the only useful animal feature.

activities.explanation: This is right because animal groups may use food, place, colour, or movement.

activities.prompt: A plant has hard woody stems that branch close to the ground. Which change would make its stem pattern fit trees instead of shrubs?
options: The stem becomes tall, thick, brown, and woody.
The stems keep branching close to the ground.
The stems become small, soft, and green.
The stem becomes weak and needs support.

why.The stems keep branching close to the gr: This mistake keeps the stem pattern that fits shrubs.
This mistake changes the stem pattern to fit herbs.
This mistake changes the stem pattern to fit climbers.

activities.explanation: This is right because trees have tall stems with hard, thick, brown, woody parts.

activities.prompt: A class sorts many plants and animals into groups. What shows that sorting helped them study?
options: They can compare members in each group more clearly.
They can forget all differences between members.
They can put all members into one big group.
They can stop studying members in each group.

why.They can forget all differences between: This mistake thinks grouping removes all differences inside groups.
why.They can put all members into one big gr: This mistake thinks grouping should put everything into one group.
why.They can stop studying members in each g: This mistake thinks stopping the study shows better understanding.

activities.explanation: This is right. Grouping makes plants and animals easier to understand and study.

lessons.title: Leaves, Roots and Seeds

activities.prompt: What might leaves, roots and seeds reveal together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Leaves, Roots and Seeds
activities.body:
You begin your plant tour by looking closely at leaves. You may notice thin lines on the leaves of many plants. This arrangement of veins is called venation.

Some leaves have a net-like pattern of veins. This pattern is called reticulate venation. Other leaves have veins that run side by side. This arrangement shows parallel venation.

Now turn your attention from leaves to roots. The main root of a plant is called a taproot. A bunch of similar-sized thin roots is called fibrous roots. Plants with reticulate venation generally have taproots. Plants with parallel venation generally have fibrous roots.

Your tour now reaches a chickpea seed. Each part of the seed is called a cotyledon. Plants whose seeds have two cotyledons are called dicotyledons. A maize seed has one thin cotyledon. Plants with seeds like those of maize are called monocotyledons. Dicotyledons generally have reticulate venation and taproot systems. Now you can compare a plant's leaves, roots and seeds.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Patterns in Leaves, Roots and Seeds
activities.body: Many plant leaves have thin lines. The pattern of these lines is called venation. A net-like pattern is called reticulate venation. Veins that run side by side are parallel venation. Plants with net-like veins usually have taproots. Plants with parallel veins usually have fibrous roots. Each part of a chickpea seed is a cotyledon. Plants with two cotyledons are dicotyledons. A maize (corn) seed has one thin cotyledon. Plants with seeds like maize are monocotyledons.
keyPoints: Leaves have net-like or side-by-side veins.
Leaf veins usually match taproots or fibrous roots.
Cotyledons help us name dicotyledons and monocotyledons.
activities.explanation: These patterns help you sort leaves, roots and seeds.

activities.prompt: Two potted plants have leaves with different vein patterns. What root systems should be expected?
steps: One leaf has a net-like pattern, which is reticulate venation.
A reticulate-veined plant generally has a taproot, so the first plant should have one main root.
The other leaf has side-by-side veins, which shows parallel venation.
A parallel-veined plant generally has fibrous roots, so the second plant should have a bunch of similar-sized thin roots.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Seeds and Plant Groups
activities.body: Plants can be grouped by their seed parts. Each part of a chickpea seed is called a cotyledon. Plants with two cotyledons are called dicotyledons. A maize seed has one thin cotyledon. Plants with maize-like seeds are called monocotyledons. Dicots usually have reticulate venation and taproot systems. Parallel-veined plants usually have fibrous roots.
keyPoints: A chickpea seed has parts called cotyledons.
Two cotyledons mean a dicotyledon.
Maize-like seeds belong to monocotyledons.
activities.explanation: Seed parts and leaf patterns give useful clues about plants.

activities.title: A Leaf with a Net
activities.prompt: Imagine a leaf. Its veins make a net. Which description shows its venation (the pattern of veins)?
options: Veins joined in a net
Veins running side by side
One main root
A bunch of thin roots of about the same size
activities.explanation: A pattern like a net is called reticulate venation.

activities.title: Side-by-Side Veins
activities.prompt: Veins that run side by side show parallel venation.
activities.explanation: Yes. Side-by-side veins form a parallel venation pattern.

activities.title: The Main Root
activities.prompt: The main root of a plant is called its ______.
activities.hint: This root has the special name shown in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The main root of a plant is called a taproot.

activities.title: Match the Plant Parts
activities.prompt: Match each description to its correct name.
activities.explanation: Each name describes the leaf pattern, root type or seed part shown.

activities.title: Two Cotyledons
activities.prompt: A plant has a seed with two cotyledons. What is this plant called?
options: A monocotyledon
A dicotyledon
A taproot
A fibrous root
activities.explanation: Plants with seeds that have two cotyledons are called dicotyledons.

activities.title: Match the Leaf Pattern and Roots
activities.prompt: Which pair correctly matches a leaf's venation with its usual roots?
options: Reticulate venation — fibrous roots
Parallel venation — taproot
Reticulate venation — taproot
Parallel venation — fibrous roots
activities.explanation: Parallel-veined plants generally have fibrous roots. These roots are similar-sized and thin.

activities.prompt: A gardener sees a leaf with a net-like vein pattern. What root system would the gardener generally expect?
options: The plant should have a taproot.
The plant should have fibrous roots.
The plant should have both root types.
The plant's roots cannot be predicted.

This confuses a net-like vein pattern with veins running side by side.
This assumes one plant should show both general root patterns.
This treats a general link as if no prediction were possible.

activities.explanation: This is right because reticulate venation generally goes with a taproot.

activities.prompt: A seedling comes from a seed with two cotyledons. What leaf and root pattern would you generally expect?
options: Net-like veins and a taproot.
Net-like veins and fibrous roots.
Side-by-side veins and a taproot.
Side-by-side veins and fibrous roots.

This gets the dicot leaf pattern right but confuses its usual root type.
This uses the dicot leaf pattern but pairs it with the wrong root type.
This reverses both general links between venation and root type.

activities.explanation: This is right because two cotyledons mean the plant is a dicotyledon, which generally has reticulate venation and a taproot.

activities.prompt: A plant is pulled up. It has many thin roots of about the same size. What are its leaf veins usually like?
options: The veins make a net-like pattern.
The veins run side by side.
The veins all meet at one point.
The veins form no clear pattern.

This is wrong. Fibrous roots usually go with parallel veins.
This makes up a leaf pattern. The roots do not show it.
This thinks fibrous roots give no useful clue.

activities.explanation: This mixes up fibrous roots with reticulate venation (net-like veins).

activities.prompt: After seeing a reticulate-veined plant, a student predicts its roots. Which prediction matches the lesson best?
options: It will probably have a taproot, as a general rule.
It will certainly have a taproot in every case.
It will probably have fibrous roots, as a general rule.
It cannot have any kind of root system.

why.It will certainly have a taproot in ever: This turns a general link into a certain rule.
why.It will probably have fibrous roots, as: This reverses the general link between venation and roots.
This treats an unsupported claim as impossible.

activities.explanation: This is right because the lesson gives a general link, not an absolute rule.

lessons.title: Grouping Animals and Changing Surroundings

activities.prompt: What can we learn by comparing animals and their surroundings?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Animals, Regions and Protection
activities.body:
Welcome to a wildlife tour. You will group animals by looking at their bodies, movement and surroundings. Animals differ greatly from one another. Some fly, run, crawl, walk, hop or jump. Each uses different body parts to move.

Now look at fish in water. Their streamlined bodies and fins help them move. Goats live in grassy areas and use their legs to move. You can compare these animals and notice how their bodies suit their lives.

Different animals live in different surroundings. Plants and animals found in one kind of region differ from those found elsewhere. Grouping animals helps you understand their diversity.

Next, you meet Janaki Ammal, an Indian botanist who worked for environmental protection. She helped document and preserve India's rich plant biodiversity.

You then visit Silent Valley, where people opposed a hydroelectric dam across the Kunthipuzha river. Their movement succeeded in saving Silent Valley. Your tour ends with a big lesson. Animals and plants differ from one region to another. You can group animals to understand their diversity.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Animals Move in Different Ways
activities.body: Animals are very different. They move in many ways. Some fly. Some run. Some crawl, walk, hop or jump. They use different body parts to move. Grouping animals helps us understand their variety. Biodiversity means this variety of life. Different animals live in different places. Fish have smooth bodies and fins to swim. Goats live in grassy places and walk on their legs. The Silent Valley movement saved Silent Valley.
keyPoints: Animals move in different ways.
Different body parts help animals move.
Animals live in different places.
activities.explanation: Learning how animals move helps us group them.

activities.prompt: A fish and a goat are moved to a place with deep water but very little grass. Which animal is better suited to move around there, and why?
steps: The fish is better suited because its streamlined body and fins help it move in water.
The goat is less suited there because it lives in grassy areas and uses its legs to move.
This shows that different animals have different body parts and live in different surroundings.
Grouping animals by movement and surroundings helps us understand their diversity because it shows what makes them different.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: Match each animal or group with its movement features.
activities.explanation: Fish use streamlined bodies and fins in water. Goats live in grassy areas and use their legs.

It helps us understand their diversity.
It changes where every animal lives.
It makes every animal move faster.
activities.explanation: Grouping animals helps us understand their diversity. It shows how greatly animals differ.

The Silent Valley movement opposed the dam
The movement succeeded in saving Silent Valley
activities.explanation: The movement opposed the dam across the Kunthipuzha river. It succeeded in saving Silent Valley.

Goats use streamlined bodies and fins in water.
Both animals live in the same places.
Plants and animals are the same in every place.

lessons.title: Adaptations and Habitats

activities.prompt: How do plants and animals find surprising ways to survive in different places?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Surviving in Different Habitats
activities.body:
Imagine that you are visiting different habitats. You soon notice that each place has its own needs. A habitat is where plants and animals live. It provides food, water, air, shelter, and other needs for survival.

Now, step into a hot desert. Very little water is available here. Desert plants store water in their fleshy stems. These helpful features let plants and animals survive in a region. Such features are called adaptations.

Next, meet a hot-desert camel. It has long legs and wide hooves. It has one hump, and it does not sweat. These adaptations help it live where very little water is available.

Travel onwards to a cold desert. A cold-desert camel has shorter legs and two humps. Its shorter legs help it walk easily in mountainous regions. Nearby, deodar trees have a conical shape and sloping branches.

Finally, compare the variety around you. Biodiversity varies from region to region because conditions are different. You begin to see why special features matter in each habitat.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Living in a Habitat
activities.body: Plants and animals live in a habitat. A habitat gives food, water, air and shelter. Special features that help them survive are called adaptations. Deserts have very little water. Desert plants can store water in thick stems. Deodar trees have a cone-like shape and sloping branches.
keyPoints: A habitat is where plants and animals live.
Habitats give living things what they need.
Adaptations are special features that help living things survive.
activities.explanation: Habitats give living things what they need to survive.

activities.prompt: Look at two camels. One camel has one hump, long legs and wide hooves. The other camel has two humps and shorter legs. Which camel lives in a hot desert? Which camel lives in a cold desert?
steps: The one-humped camel fits a hot desert. Hot-desert camels have one hump, long legs and wide hooves.
The two-humped camel fits a cold desert. Cold-desert camels have two humps and shorter legs.
Shorter legs suit the cold desert. They help the camel walk easily in the mountains.
So each camel has features for its habitat (where it lives). These features help it survive there.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: What is the place where plants and animals live called?
options: A habitat
An adaptation
A hump
A fleshy stem
activities.explanation: A habitat is the place where plants and animals live.

activities.prompt: Match each plant or animal with its special feature.
pairs: Have conical shapes and sloping branches
activities.explanation: Each pair matches a plant or animal with its special feature.

activities.prompt: Camels of hot deserts have long legs and wide ______.
activities.hint: Think about the part of a camel that touches the ground.
activities.explanation: Wide hooves are an adaptation of camels in hot deserts.

activities.prompt: Which camel can walk easily in mountainous regions?
options: A hot-desert camel
A cold-desert camel
Both kinds of camel
Neither kind of camel
activities.explanation: Cold-desert camels have shorter legs that help them walk easily in mountainous regions.

activities.prompt: Why does biodiversity vary from region to region?
options: Every region has the same conditions.
All regions have very little water.
Conditions are different.
Plants and animals have no habitats.
activities.explanation: Different conditions lead to different biodiversity in different regions.

activities.prompt: Deodar trees have a ______ shape and sloping branches.
activities.hint: Their shape is like a cone.
activities.explanation: Deodar trees have a conical shape and sloping branches.

activities.prompt: A park receives two camels. One has one hump, long legs and wide hooves. The other has two humps and shorter legs. Which came from a hot desert?
options: The camel with one hump and long legs
The camel with two humps and shorter legs
The camel with one hump and shorter legs
The camel with two humps and long legs

why.The camel with two humps and shorter leg: Two humps and shorter legs point to a cold-desert camel.
why.The camel with one hump and shorter legs: This mixes the one hump of a hot desert with the legs of a cold desert.
why.The camel with two humps and long legs: This mixes the two humps of a cold desert with the legs of a hot desert.

activities.explanation: Hot-desert camels have one hump, long legs and wide hooves.

activities.prompt: A desert has very little water. A plant with a thick, juicy stem lives there. A child says its stem and its desert are both adaptations. What is the best fix?
options: The stem is an adaptation, and the desert is its habitat.
The stem is a habitat, and the desert is an adaptation.
The stem and the desert are both adaptations.
The stem and the desert are both habitats.

why.The stem is a habitat, and the desert is: This mixes up adaptation and habitat.
why.The stem and the desert are both adaptat: The stem helps the plant. The desert is where the plant lives.
why.The stem and the desert are both habitat: The stem stores water. The desert is where the plant lives.

activities.explanation: The juicy stem stores water. So it is an adaptation. The desert is where the plant lives. So it is its habitat.

activities.prompt: A place has very little water. A gardener sees a fleshy-stem plant and a conical plant with sloping branches. Which plant has the stated way to store water?
options: The plant with the fleshy stem
The plant with the conical shape
The plant with the sloping branches
Both of the plants can do this

why.The plant with the conical shape: A conical shape is a deodar feature, not the stated water store.
why.The plant with the sloping branches: Sloping branches are a deodar feature, not the stated water store.
why.Both of the plants can do this: Only the fleshy-stem plant is described as storing water in this way.

activities.explanation: Desert plants can store water in their fleshy stems.

activities.prompt: A place gives animals food, water, air and shelter. A camel lives in the same place. It has long legs and wide hooves. Which sentence is true?
options: The place is a habitat; its legs are adaptations.
The place is an adaptation; its legs are a habitat.
Both the place and its legs are adaptations.
Both the place and its legs are habitats.

why.The place is an adaptation; its legs are: This mixes up habitat and adaptation.
why.Both the place and its legs are adaptati: A place is not a body feature that helps an animal survive.
why.Both the place and its legs are habitats: Legs are special body features, not places where animals live.

activities.explanation: The place gives things animals need. Special body features are adaptations.

lessons.title: Protecting Habitats and Biodiversity

activities.prompt: How could we protect the many homes of life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Protecting Habitats
activities.body:
You begin your journey across land and water. Land habitats are called terrestrial habitats. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.

A frog shows you how different habitats can meet. Frogs can live in water as well as on land. Animals that can live both in water and on land are called amphibians.

Next, you see what happens when people damage these places. Damage takes away homes, food and other resources. Human activities cause the loss of natural habitats.

Good news surrounds you. Project Tiger was initiated in 1973. The Cheetah Reintroduction Project was initiated in 2022. It aims to restore the cheetah population. Great Indian Bustard habitats have been declared protected areas.

Sacred groves show you another way to care. They are undisturbed patches of forest. Nobody is allowed to harm animals or cut trees in sacred groves. Protecting biodiversity helps our planet remain full of life.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Habitats and Living Things
activities.body: A habitat is a place where plants and animals live. Land habitats are on land. Aquatic habitats are in water. Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats. Frogs live in water and on land. Animals that live in both are called amphibians. Protecting habitats keeps homes and food safe. It also protects biodiversity, the many kinds of living things.
keyPoints: Plants and animals have terrestrial (land) habitats.
Ponds, lakes, rivers and oceans are aquatic habitats.
Animals that live in water and on land are amphibians.
activities.explanation: These ideas show why habitats need protection.

activities.prompt: A family wants to clear plants around a pond where frogs live. What could happen, and what should they do?
steps: The pond is an aquatic habitat and the nearby land is a terrestrial habitat, so both are habitats.
Frogs are amphibians, so they can use both the water and the land.
Clearing plants can cause habitat loss, and damaged habitats take away homes, food, and other resources.
The family should protect both places, because protecting biodiversity helps our planet remain full of life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

Clear plants from both habitats.
Move all animals away from them.
Cut trees from the forest.

lessons.title: What We Eat and Regional Food

activities.prompt: What might you taste on a food tour across India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Regional Food
activities.body:
Imagine setting off on a food tour across India. Food is essential to daily life.

You soon notice that people in different places eat a variety of foods. You will see that each state's traditional food is usually based on crops grown there. India is an agricultural country with many kinds of soil and climate. Different crops grow according to each region's soil and climate. Local harvests help shape the traditional food of a state.

In Punjab, you might eat makki di roti, sarson da saag, or chhole bhature. In Karnataka, your plate may hold idli, dosa, sambhar, or coconut chutney. Some listed crops in Manipur include rice, bamboo, and soya bean.

Food items may arrive in many states, while others are eaten in just one state. Taste, culture, and traditions also guide regional choices.

During your tour, remember that healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities. Local traditions and available crops help explain what people eat.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Food Around Us
activities.body: Healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities. Food is essential in daily life. People in different places eat a variety of foods. Some food items are eaten in many different states, while others are eaten in only one particular state. A state's traditional food is usually based on crops grown there. Soil and climate affect crops. Taste, culture and traditions also affect regional food choices.
keyPoints: Healthy eating includes wholesome food in moderate quantities.
Regional food choices are linked with crops, soil and climate.
Taste, culture and traditions affect what people eat.
activities.explanation: These facts connect healthy eating with regional food and crops.

activities.prompt: A family moves to a region with different soil and weather. Why might its traditional food change?
steps: Compare the new soil and weather. Crops grow based on the conditions of the region.
Look at the crops grown there. A state's traditional food is usually based on those crops.
Think about taste, culture and traditions. They can also shape what people choose to eat.
So local farming often explains traditional food. Culture helps explain food choices.

options: People everywhere eat exactly the same foods.

activities.explanation: People in different places eat a variety of foods. Traditional food usually uses crops grown there.

activities.explanation: Yes. Crops grown in an area usually shape its traditional food.

lessons.title: How Cooking Practices Have Changed

activities.prompt: How would your cooking feel like without today's tools?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Cooking Changed
activities.body:
Imagine joining a family for a cooking lesson. You begin by learning how cooking was usually done earlier. People's food choices and methods of preparing food can be different. This difference helps you see how cooking practices have changed.

Now, step towards the old cooking area. Earlier, most cooking was done on a chulha. You watch the traditional method. Next, look at preparing ingredients. Earlier, most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta.

Now, step into a modern kitchen. Today, most people cook using a modern gas stove. An electrical grinder makes grinding easier. You compare these tools with earlier methods. This clear difference shows you traditional and modern cooking practices.

Before you leave, consider why cooking changed. Technological development is one reason cooking practices have changed. Better transport and communication have also helped change cooking practices. Your tour ends with a simple lesson. Food choices and cooking methods can differ. Which changes would you welcome in your own kitchen?
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Cooking Then and Now
activities.body: Traditional practices are old ways of cooking. Modern practices are ways of cooking used today. In the past, most people cooked on a chulha. Today, most people use a modern gas stove. In the past, most grinding was done by hand with a sil-batta. Today, an electric grinder makes grinding easier. Technology, transport and communication have helped cooking practices change.
keyPoints: Traditional and modern cooking practices are different.
Cooking and grinding methods have changed.
Technology, transport and communication helped these changes.
activities.explanation: Cooking practices have changed. The reasons and methods are clear.

activities.prompt: How has grinding food and cooking changed, from the past to today?
steps: In the past, most people ground food by hand with a sil-batta. This was the usual way.
Today, most people cook on a gas stove. This is the common way now.
Today, people can also use an electric grinder. It makes grinding easier.
So the way people cook has changed. New technology is one reason. Better transport and communication also helped.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.prompt: Where did most people cook earlier?

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, Fats and Proteins

activities.prompt: What are carbohydrates, fats and proteins really for in your body?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Food
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a tour of your food. At the first stop, you meet sugar. Common sugar is also a type of carbohydrate. You remember that sugar belongs to this group.

Your next stop brings you to oils. Many oils belong to the food component called fat. Soon, you also meet nuts. Groundnuts, walnuts, coconuts and almonds provide fat. Each one provides fat.

Keep walking, and you discover fat's special role. Fat is a source of stored energy. Your guide points to the word stored. Energy can wait inside fat, ready for later.

At the final stop, you find milk products and pulses. These are good sources of protein. You also learn that people obtain protein from both plants and animals. Protein-rich foods help the body grow and repair itself. Your tour ends as you understand the different jobs.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Food Components
activities.body: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are food components. Sugar is a carbohydrate. Many oils are fats. Nuts give fat. Fat stores energy for the body. Milk products and pulses (like dal) give protein. People get protein from plants and animals. Protein helps the body grow and repair itself.
keyPoints: Sugar is a carbohydrate.
Many oils and nuts give fat.
Milk products and pulses give protein.
Fat stores energy. Protein helps growth and repair.
activities.explanation: These parts give your body energy. They help it grow.

lessons.title: Vitamins, Minerals, Roughage and Water

activities.prompt: What might your food be secretly helping you do?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Your Food
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a tour through the food on your plate. You meet vitamins and minerals, which are protective nutrients. They help your body function and stay healthy.

Your guide points to vitamins A, B1, C and D. It also shows you calcium, iodine and iron. Lemons and oranges contain vitamin C. Scurvy is caused by a lack of vitamin C.

At the salt shop, you see iodised salt. It is common salt mixed with the required amount of iodine salts. Nearby, a guide explains that goitre causes swelling at the front of the neck.

Then you visit the cooking pot. Some nutrients can be lost when food is cooked at high heat. Food components are called nutrients when they help your body function and stay healthy.

Finally, you follow roughage through your digestive journey. Dietary fibre is an essential part of food, even though it provides no nutrients. It helps food move smoothly through your body. Your tour ends with a full plate of new knowledge.

activities.title: Nutrients that protect you
activities.body: Vitamins and minerals are nutrients. They help your body work and stay healthy. The chapter lists vitamins A, B1, C and D. It also lists the minerals calcium, iodine and iron. Lemons and oranges give vitamin C. Not having enough vitamin C causes scurvy. Iodised salt is common salt with iodine added. Dietary fibre gives no nutrients. But it helps food move smoothly through your body.
keyPoints: The vitamins listed are A, B1, C and D.
The minerals listed are calcium, iodine and iron.
Dietary fibre helps food move smoothly. It gives no nutrients.
activities.explanation: Vitamins, minerals and dietary fibre are all important for food and health.

activities.prompt: A cook says oranges and iodised salt protect health. But dietary fibre has no nutrients. Why should dietary fibre still be part of our food?
steps: Oranges contain vitamin C, and a lack of vitamin C causes scurvy, so this vitamin helps protect health.
Iodised salt contains iodine salts, and iodine is listed as a mineral, so minerals also help protect health.
Dietary fibre provides no nutrients, yet it is essential and helps food move smoothly through the body.
Therefore, vitamins and minerals protect health, while dietary fibre has a different but essential job.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

lessons.title: Testing Food for Nutrients

activities.prompt: What secrets are hiding inside the food we eat?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Food Testing Tour
activities.body:
You begin your food testing tour with starch, fat and protein. Each has a fairly simple testing method. You take turns using these methods on food items.

For starch, you place diluted iodine solution on each food item. You use two or three drops each time. A blue-black colour then shows that the food contains starch.

Next, you look for fat. Oil or butter leaves an oily patch on paper. An oily patch shows that the food item contains fat. Light can faintly shine through the oily patch.

For protein, you add water to each test tube and shake the mixture well. You then add two drops of copper sulfate solution to each tube. A violet colour shows that the food item contains proteins.

You must handle the chemicals used in the protein test carefully. Some other nutrients can only be detected in a well-equipped laboratory.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Food Shows Nutrients
activities.body: Food can be tested for starch, fat and protein. For starch, diluted iodine solution is placed on the food. A blue-black colour shows starch. For fat, oil or butter leaves an oily patch on paper. For protein, water is added and the mixture is shaken well. Copper sulfate solution is added. A violet colour shows proteins. Other nutrients need a well-equipped laboratory. Protein-test chemicals need careful handling.
keyPoints: Blue-black colour shows starch.
An oily patch shows fat.
Violet colour shows proteins.
activities.explanation: Different test results help us find nutrients in food.

steps: Two or three drops of diluted iodine are put on the food. This is a simple test for starch.
If the food turns blue-black, it contains starch. Blue-black shows that starch is there.
If the food is not blue-black, the child cannot say it has starch. Blue-black is needed to show starch.
So the blue-black food has starch. The child cannot say the same for the other food.

lessons.title: Balanced Diet, Millets and Food Miles

activities.prompt: What can a simple lunch reveal about food, farms and your body?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lunch, Millets and Food Miles
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a school lesson with a simple packed lunch. You look at its foods and wonder what your body needs. Your nutrient needs may change with age, gender, physical activity and health.

You discover that a balanced diet contains essential nutrients, roughage and water. It provides these in the right amounts. Foods high in sugar and fat but low in useful nutrients are called junk foods.

Junk foods are not healthy for the body. Eating junk foods often can make a person obese.

You then visit a millet field and see why millets matter. Millets contribute significantly to a balanced diet for normal body functioning. You also spot iodised salt and some baby foods on a shop shelf. These are examples of fortified foods. Adding nutrients during food processing improves the food's nutritional quality.

Next, you follow your lunch from producer to consumer. Food miles measure the distance food travels from producer to consumer. Reducing food miles can support local farmers and keep food fresh and healthy. The FSSAI also helps regulate food quality in India.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What Makes Food Healthy?
activities.body: A balanced diet has nutrients, roughage and water. It has them in the right amounts. Your needs can change with age, gender, activity and health. Millets are very helpful for a balanced diet. Junk food has a lot of sugar and fat. It has few useful nutrients. Eating junk food often can make a person obese.
keyPoints: A balanced diet has nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts.
Millets are very helpful for a balanced diet.
Eating junk food often can make a person obese.
activities.explanation: Good food choices help your body get what it needs.

activities.prompt: A child often eats a sugary, fatty snack. Another meal has nutrients, roughage and water in good amounts. Which choice is better for the body, and why?
steps: The sugary, fatty snack is junk food. It has few useful nutrients.
Junk food is not healthy. So it is not the better choice.
Eating it often can make a person obese (very fat). So it is an even worse choice.
The other meal is balanced. It has nutrients, roughage and water in good amounts. So it is the better choice.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

activities.title: Closer Food and Better Quality
activities.body: Food miles show how far food travels. It goes from the producer to the consumer. The producer grows or makes the food. The consumer buys and eats it. Cutting food miles can help local farmers. It can also keep food fresh and healthy. Fortified foods have nutrients added when they are made. This makes their nutrition better. Iodised salt and some baby foods are examples of fortified foods. The FSSAI makes rules for food quality in India.
keyPoints: Food miles measure how far food travels.
Fortified foods have added nutrients. They are better for health.
The FSSAI makes rules for food quality in India.
activities.explanation: Food from nearby, and better food, can help everyone.

activities.prompt: Which choice describes a balanced diet?
options: Essential nutrients, roughage and water in any amounts.
Only essential nutrients, without roughage or water.
Essential nutrients, roughage and water in the right amounts.
Mostly sugar and fat, with few useful nutrients.
activities.explanation: A balanced diet has all these in the right amounts.

activities.prompt: Food miles measure the ______ food travels from producer to consumer.
activities.hint: Food miles tell you how far food has travelled.
activities.explanation: Food miles measure the distance food travels from producer to you.

activities.explanation: Each pair connects a food term with the correct fact.

activities.explanation: Reducing food miles can support local farmers and keep food fresh and healthy.

The food is fortified; the FSSAI checks food quality in India.
activities.explanation: Adding nutrients to food makes it healthier. Iodised salt is fortified. FSSAI checks food quality in India.

activities.explanation: Food starts with the producer. It travels to the consumer. Its distance is measured in food miles.

activities.prompt: A first plate has nutrients, roughage and water. Its amounts are wrong. A second plate has the same three, in the right amounts. Which plate is balanced, and why?

lessons.title: Magnets and Magnetic Materials

activities.prompt: What will you discover when you explore the world of magnets?

activities.title: A Magnet Tour
activities.body:
Imagine you are travelling when the stars cannot be seen. You hold a magnetic compass. It helps you find directions. Your journey continues with a useful guide.

Long ago, people discovered lodestones. These are naturally occurring magnets. Later, people learned that magnets could also be made from iron. Magnets like this are artificial magnets.

Now you visit a shelf of colourful objects. Magnets appear in pencil boxes, stickers and toys. They are artificial magnets. You also see that magnets can be made in many different shapes.

As you explore, you test each object. Some objects are attracted to a magnet and stick to it. Materials attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic materials. You learn that iron is a magnetic material. At your next stop, you watch an iron object move towards a nearby magnet.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the Magnets
activities.body: Travellers used a magnetic compass to find directions. They did this when they could not see the stars. Lodestones are natural magnets. People found them long ago. Later, people learned to make magnets from iron. Magnets in pencil boxes, stickers and toys are artificial magnets. Artificial means made by people. Magnets can have many shapes. A magnet attracts (pulls) some objects. They stick to it. Materials that stick to magnets are called magnetic materials. Iron is a magnetic material.
keyPoints: A magnetic compass helps travellers find directions.
Lodestones are natural magnets.
Iron is a magnetic material.
activities.explanation: Magnets can be natural, artificial or made from iron.

Iron is a magnetic material, so iron is attracted towards a magnet. Magnets can be made in many different shapes. People can make magnets from iron. Artificial magnets are used in pencil boxes, stickers and toys.

Attracted materials are called magnetic materials.
Iron is attracted towards a magnet.
activities.explanation: Magnetic materials are attracted towards magnets, and iron is one of them.

lessons.title: The Poles of a Magnet

activities.prompt: What happens if you break a magnet into tiny pieces?

activities.title: A Tour of the Magnet’s Poles
activities.body:
Imagine entering a science room with a bar magnet and a tray of iron filings. You gently sprinkle them over the magnet. Many cling near its ends, while only a few stick along the rest. The ends are the North pole and the South pole.

Now you move the magnet towards scattered filings. The greatest number gather near the two ends. Few filings stick to the remaining part. You have found where the filings gather most.

Then you wonder whether you can keep just one end. You try breaking the bar magnet into smaller pieces. Every smaller piece becomes a magnet. Each has its own North pole and South pole.

You look closely and notice something surprising. North and South poles always exist in pairs. A single North pole or a single South pole cannot exist. It is not possible to obtain a magnet with only one pole.

Each broken piece remains a magnet with both poles. Your experiment ends with this surprising discovery.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Meet the Magnet's Poles
activities.body: A bar magnet has two poles. One is the North pole. The other is the South pole. Iron filings are tiny pieces of iron. Most iron filings stick near the ends of the magnet. Only a few stick to the middle part. If you break a magnet, each piece still has two poles. So, one pole alone cannot exist.
keyPoints: The poles are the North pole and the South pole.
Most iron filings stick near the magnet's ends.
Every smaller magnet still has both poles.
activities.explanation: The ends hold the most iron filings, and every magnet keeps both poles.

lessons.title: Using a Suspended Magnet to Find Directions

activities.prompt: Could a hanging magnet help you find your way?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Magnet Finds the Way
activities.body:
You tie a thread around the middle of a bar magnet. Then you let it hang freely. First, turn it gently in the horizontal direction. After this, leave it to rest.

As the magnet settles, look along the line through its resting ends. This line shows its north-south direction. Turn the magnet again, then let it rest once more. It rests along the same line.

The end pointing north is called the North-seeking pole, or North pole. The end pointing south is called the South-seeking pole, or South pole. The Earth behaves like a giant magnet, guiding the suspended magnet.

Now try a small iron bar in the same way. It can rest in any direction because it is not a magnet. Only magnets rest along the north-south direction. A freely suspended magnet therefore shows you the north-south line.

This north-south resting property helps you find directions. You can use your suspended magnet to identify the north-south direction.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Magnet That Finds North and South
activities.body: Tie a thread around the middle of a bar magnet to suspend it. Turn it gently in the horizontal direction, then leave it to rest. The end pointing north is the North pole. The end pointing south is the South pole.

activities.explanation: The magnet's resting line reveals north and south.

lessons.title: Making and Using a Magnetic Compass

activities.prompt: How could you make a tiny compass with simple materials?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Your First Magnetic Compass
activities.body:
You place an iron sewing needle on a wooden table. It looks simple, but it can become a compass. A magnetic compass holds a needle-shaped magnet. This magnet can rotate freely.

Take one pole of a magnet. Stroke the needle with it at least 30 to 40 times. Then test the needle with some pins. If pins or iron filings stick, the needle has become a magnet.

The attracted pins show that your needle is now magnetised. Next, pass it through a cork horizontally. The needle should rest across the cork. This makes a simple floating compass.

Float the cork and needle in a glass bowl filled with water. The magnetised needle can rotate freely on the water. Your simple magnetic compass is ready.

Long ago, Indians used a similar magnetic device for navigation at sea. The old device held a magnetised fish-shaped iron piece in oil. Your cork compass uses the same simple magnetic idea.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.body: A magnetic compass has a needle. The needle is a small magnet. It can turn freely. To make one, put an iron sewing needle on a wooden table. Rub it with one pole (end) of a magnet. Do this 30 to 40 times. If pins or iron filings stick, the needle is a magnet. Next, push the needle sideways through a cork. Float the cork and needle in water.

Rubbing it with one pole makes the needle magnetic.
The magnetised needle sits in a cork and floats on water.
activities.explanation: Start with the needle. Magnetise it. Then float it on the cork.

lessons.title: Attraction and Repulsion between Magnets

activities.prompt: What will you discover when two magnets meet?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Magnetic Behaviour
activities.body:
You enter a tiny magnet workshop and hold two magnets. You bring their ends close together. A North pole attracts a South pole. The magnets move towards each other. But North poles repel each other. South poles repel each other too.

Next, you meet an iron bar. Both ends of the bar are attracted by a magnet. The magnet’s North and South poles attract both ends. You watch the bar respond to either pole.

Then you visit a magnetic compass. Its needle is also a magnet. Bring a North pole near the needle’s North pole. The needle moves away. Bring a South pole near that North pole. The needle moves closer.

You wonder how to check whether an object is a magnet. Repulsion can identify it. You hold the object near another magnet. A push-away response shows that it repels the magnet.

Finally, you place wood, cardboard, plastic or glass between the compass and a magnet. There is no appreciable change in the needle’s deflection. The magnetic effect can pass through non-magnetic materials. You watch the response through each material.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Like and Unlike Poles
activities.body: Like poles repel each other. Repel means push away. Two North poles push apart. Two South poles push apart too. Unlike poles attract each other. Attract means pull together. A North pole pulls towards a South pole. A magnet attracts both ends of an iron bar. A compass needle is also a magnet. So it can show these pushes and pulls.
keyPoints: A North pole and a South pole attract each other.
Two North poles repel each other.
Two South poles repel each other.
activities.explanation: Magnets attract unlike poles. They repel like poles.

activities.takeaway: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel, and magnets have a stronger effect when they are close.
activities.explanation: Unlike poles attract, like poles repel, and magnets have a stronger effect when they are close.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: 5.1 measuring with body parts; 5.2 standard units of length; 5.3 measuring length correctly; 5.4 curved lines and 5.5 describing position.

lessons.title: 5.1 Measuring with Body Parts

activities.prompt: Why might your body be useful for measuring?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Body Measures
activities.body:
You visit Deepa's grandmother. She measures cloth using the length of her arm. You wonder how her arm helps her measure the cloth.

Next, you meet a farmer. He can measure land by walking and counting his strides. Farmers may also use the length of their feet. You consider two ways to measure.

Then you visit Deepa's mother. She calls a handspan a balisht. Soon, five friends test their handspans. You find that their handspans have different lengths. The number of handspans needed for the table is different for everyone.

Now you learn how to describe a measured length. It needs a number and a unit. In 13 handspans, 13 is the number and handspan is the unit. A standard unit should give the same measurement for everyone measuring the same length.

Finally, you see scales and measuring tapes. These tools are useful because body-based units can differ between people. A standard unit helps everyone measure the same length consistently.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Measuring with Your Body
activities.body: Body-based measurements use a person’s body as a unit. A handspan is one such unit, and Deepa’s mother calls it a balisht. People can have different handspan lengths, so the same length may need different numbers of handspans. Every measured length has a number and a unit. A standard unit should give everyone the same measurement for the same length. Scales and measuring tapes are useful because body-based units can differ between people.
keyPoints: Arms, feet, strides and handspans can measure length.
A measured length has a number and a unit.
A standard unit gives the same measurement for everyone.
activities.explanation: Different handspan lengths can give different measurements.

activities.prompt: Two friends measure the same table using their own handspans. Why might their results differ, and what should be used when everyone must get the same result?
steps: The friends' handspans have different lengths, as five friends found.
Different handspan lengths can make the same table need different numbers of handspans.
A standard unit is useful for shared measuring because it should give everyone the same measurement.
Therefore, body-based measures may differ between people, while scales and measuring tapes can help people agree on a measurement.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Lumi.

lessons.title: 5.2 Standard Units of Length

activities.prompt: How do people agree on how to measure length?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Length Units
activities.body:
Your tour begins with three curious words: angula, dhanusa and yojana. These were units named in ancient Indian literature. You pause to notice that traditional carpenters and tailors still use the angula.

You now travel between countries and wonder why everyone measures alike. Travel had caused confusion about measurements, so different countries adopted shared standard units. The system used now is called the International System of Units, or SI units. Its unit of length is the metre, and its symbol is m.

You hold a metre scale and look closely. It is divided into 100 equal divisions. Each division on the scale is called a centimetre. This also shows that one metre equals 100 centimetres. Looking closer still, you find that one centimetre equals 10 millimetres.

Your tour now moves towards longer distances. One kilometre equals 1000 metres. Finally, you meet the inch and learn that one inch equals 2.54 centimetres. You finish with a clearer picture of how these units compare.

activities.title: Our shared standard units
activities.body: Different countries agreed on shared standard units. This was because travel had caused confusion about measurements. The system we use now is the International System of Units. It is called SI units for short. Its unit of length is the metre. It is written as m. A metre has 100 equal parts. Each part is called a centimetre.
keyPoints: Shared units reduce confusion when people travel.
The SI unit of length is the metre.
Each part of a metre is called a centimetre.
activities.explanation: Shared units help people everywhere measure length clearly.

Travel caused confusion about measurements. So countries chose shared standard units.

activities.prompt: What helps you measure each object accurately?
