activities.title: Your Measuring Tour
activities.body:
You begin by choosing a scale suitable for the length you need to measure. A 15-cm scale can be used to measure a pencil.

A metre scale or measuring tape may be needed to measure a room’s height. A flexible measuring tape is more suitable for measuring a tree’s girth or chest size. You match the scale to each length before you begin measuring.

You place the scale beside the object so it touches the object along its length. You keep your eye directly above the tip of the object while reading the scale. If the zero mark is unclear, you use another full mark on the scale.

You use a flexible measuring tape or thread to measure a curved line. If you use thread, you straighten it before measuring its length with a metre scale.

Finally, you write down the measurement. A written measurement must include both a number and its unit. Your tour ends with a measurement that includes its unit.

If the zero mark is not clear, use another whole number mark. A measurement needs a number and a unit. A unit is like cm or m. For curved lines, use a flexible tape or thread.

activities.title: Reference Points for Distance
activities.body:
You meet friends who compare how far places are from their homes. Their observations differ because each child measures from a different house. Their observations would agree if they measured from the same object or point. You call this fixed object or point a reference point.

Now you help the friends plan a Kabaddi court. They plan to draw its lines with chuna powder. First, they choose one point on the ground. They will measure all distances from this point.

Next, you see kilometre stones while Padma moves closer to Delhi. A kilometre stone shows that Delhi is 70 km away. The next kilometre stone shows that Delhi is 60 km away. The decreasing numbers show that Padma is getting closer to Delhi.

You now describe Padma’s position by using Delhi as the reference point. When the stone reads 70 km, Padma’s position is 70 km from Delhi. When the stone reads 60 km, Padma’s position is 60 km from Delhi.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Measuring from a Reference Point
activities.body: Distance can look different when people measure from different houses. Their results can match if they measure from the same object or point. A starting point that does not move is a reference point. Padma used Delhi as her reference point. The stones on the road showed 70 km, then 60 km. Padma was getting closer to Delhi.
keyPoints: Distance measurements can be different.
A reference point is a starting point that does not move.
Padma measured her distance from Delhi.
activities.explanation: A reference point gives everyone the same starting place for distances.

activities.prompt: Two children measure the distance to one tree. Each child starts from their own house. Why do their answers differ? How can they get the same answer?
steps: One child measures from one house. The other measures from another house.
Their answers can differ. Each child has a different starting point.
If both children start at the same house, their answers will match. They use the same starting point.
The same starting point is the reference point for both. A reference point is where you start measuring.
activities.explanation: Think about it with Lumi.

lessons.title: 5.6 Moving Things

activities.prompt: What could change your view about moving things?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Moving Things
activities.body:
You join Deepa as she watches the passengers inside a moving bus. After a minute, the passengers are still in their seats. Their positions are not changing with time, so they seem at rest.

Now you choose the bus as the reference point. This helps you decide whether an object is at rest or in motion. Compared with the bus, the passengers are at rest.

Next, you look towards a building outside the bus. You use its position as the reference point. From the building’s position, both the passengers and the bus are moving.

After this tour, you see that motion depends on your chosen reference point. You also meet objects that may travel in straight lines. A falling eraser may move along a straight line. An orange dropped from a tree may do the same. Students marching in a parade may move on a straight-line path. A heavy box that is pushed may move along a straight line.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Motion and Reference Points
activities.body: Motion depends on the reference point you choose. A reference point is a thing you compare with. A reference point helps us see if something is moving. If it is not moving, it is at rest (still). Use the bus as the reference point. The people on the bus stayed in their seats. So they were at rest. Now use a building outside as the reference point. Then the bus and the people were both moving.
keyPoints: Motion depends on the reference point you choose.
The people were at rest, compared to the bus.
The bus and the people were moving, compared to a building.
activities.explanation: A good reference point helps you see motion clearly.

activities.prompt: A child says: 'The passengers are not moving. But the bus is moving.' How can both be true?
steps: Choose the bus as the reference point. A reference point is what we compare with.
The passengers sit in their seats. Their place does not change. So they are at rest compared to the bus.
Choose a building outside the bus as a new reference point.
Compared to the building, the passengers and the bus are both moving. So both statements can be true.

activities.title: Moving Along a Straight Line

A dropped orange may move in a straight line.
Marching students and a pushed box may also move straight.
activities.explanation: Different moving objects may share a straight-line path.

activities.explanation: From the building's position, both the passengers and the bus were moving.

lessons.title: 5.7 Types of Motion

activities.prompt: Ready to explore what helps us tell different kinds of motion apart?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Types of Motion
activities.body:
Imagine a tour of motion. You move along a straight line. This is called linear motion. Soon, you enter a circular path. This is called circular motion. An object in circular motion travels around the circular path again and again.

Here, you meet motion to and fro. This is called oscillatory motion. An object in oscillatory motion repeats its movement to and fro. Oscillatory motion is periodic, just like circular motion.

Periodic motion means an object repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. Circular and oscillatory motion are both periodic. They repeat their paths again and again.

Now, you press a metal strip. Its free end moves up and down. You also see an eraser moving on a thread. This movement is similar to a swing. You can classify motion as linear, circular or oscillatory.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Motion has different types
activities.body: Linear motion means moving along a straight line. Circular motion means moving around in a circle. Oscillatory motion means moving back and forth around one place. Periodic motion repeats its path after a fixed interval of time. A fixed interval means the same time gap every time. Both circular and oscillatory motion are periodic.
keyPoints: Linear motion goes along a straight line.
Circular and oscillatory motions repeat their movement.
Periodic motion repeats its path after a fixed interval of time.
activities.explanation: You can sort motion by its path or pattern.

activities.prompt: One toy moves on a straight track. One toy goes around a circle. One toy moves back and forth around one fixed point. How can you tell their motion types apart? What do they share?
steps: First, watch the first toy's path. A path on one straight line is linear motion.
Next, watch the second toy's path. Going around a circle is circular motion.
Then watch the third toy. Moving back and forth around one point is oscillatory motion.
Last, compare what repeats. Circular and oscillatory motion are both periodic.

activities.prompt: Both circular and oscillatory motion are periodic.
activities.explanation: True! Circular motion repeats around a path. Oscillatory motion also repeats to and fro.

activities.prompt: Put these steps in order. They show why circular motion is periodic.
items: The object moves around the circle.
The object goes around the path again and again.
The path repeats after the same amount of time.
activities.explanation: Circular motion goes around the same path again and again. Motion that repeats after the same time is periodic motion.

activities.prompt: Which answer tells what linear motion is, and which motions are periodic?
options: Linear means round motion; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Linear means oscillatory motion; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Linear means staying still; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
Linear means straight-line motion; circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.
activities.explanation: Linear motion goes in a straight line. Circular and oscillatory motions are periodic.

lessons.title: 1. Observing Objects Around Us

activities.prompt: What stories are hiding in the materials of objects around you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Materials
activities.body:
Begin your tour by looking at objects around you. Ask what each one is made from. A material is any substance used to create an object. Everyday objects are made from various materials, and paper is one of them.

Next, travel back to early pottery. The earliest pottery found in the Ganga plains dates back to 7,000 to 8,000 years. It was also found in Baluchistan at Mehrgarh.

Now, meet the Sindhu-Sarasvatī people. They developed wheel-turned pottery techniques about 4000 BCE onwards. Their Harappan pottery had a bright red surface painted with black-coloured designs.

Watch the making process with care. Makers carefully selected the clay used for pots, dishes, bowls and other items. The prepared clay was finally baked in a kiln to make terracotta. Each stage helps turn clay into useful objects.

Finish your tour by imagining pots in daily life. Pots were used for cooking and for storing food grains, oil, ghee and other things.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Objects and Materials
activities.body: Materials are the substances used to make objects. Everyday objects are made from different materials. Paper is one such material. People also made pots, dishes and bowls from carefully selected clay. The clay was prepared and baked in a kiln to make terracotta. These pots helped with cooking and storing food.

Everyday objects are made from various materials.
Paper and clay are materials.
Prepared clay becomes terracotta when baked in a kiln.
activities.explanation: Objects tell us about the materials used to make them.

lessons.title: 2. How to Group Materials?

activities.prompt: How can you decide which objects belong together?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sorting Objects and Materials
activities.body:
Imagine you enter a room filled with objects. You want to sort them into groups, but where should you begin? Look for shared properties, such as shape, colour, hardness, softness and shine.

Classification means arranging objects into groups. Objects can be classified according to a common property. Materials can also be classified according to certain properties. You might make one group for shiny objects and another for soft objects.

One object can be made from different materials. One material can be used to make more than one object. You can group both the objects and the materials.

Think about a tumbler. Its material must be capable of holding water. You choose a material according to its properties. The purpose of an object also affects your choice of material.

Different parts of an object may use different materials. A pen may contain plastic, metal and ink. Sports balls are made from specific materials for specific sports.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How We Group Materials
activities.body: You can group objects by their properties. Properties are things like shape, colour, hardness, softness and shine. Grouping is called classification. One object can use many materials. One material can make many objects. The material we pick depends on its properties and its use. Different parts can use different materials. For example, a pen can have plastic, metal and ink.

We pick materials by their properties and use.
One object can have different materials.

lessons.title: 4. Seeing Through and Dissolving Materials

activities.prompt: What can you discover by looking through different materials?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Through Materials
activities.body:
Imagine glass before your eyes. You can see things clearly through this transparent material. The view remains clear as your eyes look beyond it.

You try air and water next. Both are transparent, and so is cellophane paper. Through each one, you can still see the things behind it clearly.

Now you meet a piece of wood. You cannot see at all through this opaque material. An opaque material stops your view completely. Cardboard and metals are opaque too.

Next, you hold butter paper. You can see objects through it, but not clearly. This material is translucent. Frosted glass is translucent too. Your view stays, but it is not sharp.

Finally, you look at water with some liquids. Some mix completely with it. Others form a separate layer because they do not mix with water. Oxygen gas dissolves in water, which is important for water-living animals and plants.

activities.body: Glass, water, air and cellophane paper are transparent. You can see clearly through transparent materials. Wood, cardboard and metals are opaque. lessons.title: 5. Mass and Volume

activities.prompt: What can you learn by comparing two different tumblers?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Mass and Volume
activities.body:
Imagine you are holding two tumblers. Both have the same capacity, but they hold different amounts of water. One holds more, while the other holds less.

Mass helps you describe whether an object is heavier or lighter. The heavier object has more mass, while the lighter object has less mass.

Water also takes up space. The space occupied by water represents its volume. Tumblers with the same capacity can hold different amounts of water, so equal capacity does not always mean equal volume.

Water bottles show another useful clue. The quantity written on each bottle tells you the volume of water it holds. You can also write volume units in a shorter way: litre is written as L, and millilitre as mL.

Mass has its own special unit. The kilogram is the SI unit used for measuring mass. Its symbol is written in lower case as kg. Cubic metre is the SI unit of volume, and one cubic metre equals 1000 litres. As you explore, remember that mass and volume are two properties possessed by all materials.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Mass and Volume
activities.body: Mass tells whether an object is heavier or lighter. More mass means heavier, and less mass means lighter. Volume is the space occupied by water. Two tumblers can have the same capacity but hold different amounts of water. Water bottles show volume in litres or millilitres, written L and mL. Mass uses the kilogram, written kg. The cubic metre is the volume unit. One cubic metre equals 1000 litres.
keyPoints: Heavier means more mass; lighter means less mass.
Volume is the space occupied by water.
Mass uses kilograms; volume uses the cubic metre.
activities.explanation: These ideas help you compare mass and volume.

lessons.title: 6. Matter and Classification

activities.prompt: How can we sort the things around us? What is matter?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Matter
activities.body:
You begin your journey by looking around you at everything that takes up space. You soon learn that anything occupying space and having mass is called matter. Mass tells you how much matter there is.

Next, you follow an object through a busy workshop. The space occupied by that matter is its volume. Materials are types of matter used when objects are created. You compare both ideas as you explore.

Then, you enter a room where things are grouped by shared properties. Grouping helps you study and observe patterns in the properties of things. The non-living world is also classified according to properties.

You also find that Ayurveda has its own system for grouping things. The Ayurvedic shloka describes twenty properties. These properties form ten pairs of opposite qualities. You now recognise these pairs as you compare different things.

At the end, you see that these properties describe all physical matter. They can also describe living systems, the environment, and food. You leave ready to explore how matter can be understood and organised.

Properties are features used to group and describe things. Grouping helps us observe patterns. Ayurveda also groups things. Its twenty properties form ten pairs of opposite qualities. These properties describe physical matter, living systems, the environment and food.

lessons.title: 7.1 Hot or Cold? Can We Always Trust Touch?

activities.prompt: The same water can feel cool to one hand. It can feel warm to the other hand. How can this be?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: When Touch Tricks You
activities.body:
You notice that some bodies are naturally hotter than others. You think of cold water from a matka. Tap water may feel hotter than that cold water. Your sense of touch cannot always judge how hot or cold things are.

You use warm water in A for an investigation. You also use tap water in B and ice-cold water in C. First, you place one hand in A. You place your other hand in C.

Next, you place both hands together in the tap water. The hand from the warm water may make it feel cool. The hand from the ice-cold water may make the same water feel warm.

Your hand can change how the same water feels. Both hands are touching the same tap water. Yet they may give you opposite feelings about it.

Touch alone cannot always decide correctly whether a body is hot or cold. You remember that your first touch may mislead you. So, you need more than touch alone.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Can we always trust touch?
activities.body: Some bodies are hotter than other bodies. Tap water may feel hotter than cold water from a matka. Touch cannot always tell us how hot or cold something is. An investigation uses warm water in A. B has tap water. C has ice-cold water. Hands placed in different water can make the same tap water feel different. Touch cannot always decide whether a body is hot or cold.
keyPoints: Some bodies are naturally hotter than others.
Different hands may change how the same tap water feels.
Touch alone cannot always decide correctly.

activities.prompt: What could help us compare how hot or cold our bodies feel?

activities.title: A Tour of Thermometers
activities.body:
You begin your science tour by wondering how people compare hotness and coldness. Temperature is a reliable measure of a body’s hotness or coldness. The difference between two temperatures shows how their hotness compares.

Next, you meet the tool that can measure it. A thermometer is a device that measures temperature. A hotter body has a higher temperature than a colder body.

Your tour now moves from general ideas to special tools. The two common kinds are clinical and laboratory thermometers. Clinical thermometers measure human body temperature. Laboratory thermometers are used for many other purposes.

You then look closely at the body-temperature thermometer. It is called a clinical thermometer. A digital clinical thermometer shows the temperature on a display. Digital clinical thermometers run on batteries.

Finally, you consider why the digital kind is helpful. Mercury is extremely toxic and can be difficult to dispose of safely. Digital thermometers avoid the risk posed by mercury. You finish your tour with a clear picture of temperature and thermometers.

activities.title: A Tour of Temperature Scales
activities.body:
Imagine that you meet three temperature scales during a friendly tour. Each scale has its own special symbol and style. You will see how to write them correctly.

Your first stop is the clinical thermometer. It cannot measure the temperatures of boiling water or ice. Next, you meet Celsius, written as degree Celsius, with the symbol °C. Fahrenheit follows, written as degree Fahrenheit, with the symbol °F.

Then comes Kelvin, written as kelvin, with the symbol K. Kelvin is the SI unit of temperature. The three scales were named after the scientists who developed them. To convert Celsius to Kelvin, add 273.15 to the Celsius value.

Now you practise the symbols. The symbols °C, °F and K all use capital letters. The degree sign is not written with the Kelvin unit. Leave a space between a temperature number and its unit.

Finally, remember the plural “degrees”. Use it when writing a temperature above one degree. You can now use the right unit and symbol with confidence.

Leave a space between a temperature number and its unit. Use degrees above one degree.

You meet a laboratory thermometer during a science lesson. You begin by looking closely at its long, narrow tube.

You may see coloured alcohol or mercury inside the thermometer. The laboratory thermometer shown has a range from –10 °C to 110 °C.

activities.prompt: Why does water sometimes seem to disappear?

activities.title: Water's Disappearing Act
activities.body:
You open the freezer and find water turned into hard ice. When you touch it, the ice feels hard. You now begin a journey through the changing forms of water.

Next, you leave the ice on a table. Soon, it becomes water. You watch this change and begin to wonder what has happened. Ice and water are two forms of the same substance.

During your tour, water flows and splashes beside you. Ice does neither. The different forms of a substance are called states. This word helps you understand the changes you see.

At the playground, some water in puddles disappears by the evening. Water left on utensils also dries up after some time. Both changes make you ask where the water has gone.

The answer is a gaseous state called water vapour. Water can change into this vapour through evaporation. You cannot see water vapour itself. When you see steam, tiny water droplets make it visible.

activities.title: Droplet Detectives
activities.body:
You hold a glass tumbler containing cold water and ice. Tiny water droplets appear on its outside. You wonder where it came from.

The small droplets combine to form bigger drops. You and the children notice that the water level did not go down. One possible reason is that some ice melted outside the glass tumbler.

During Activity 8.4, you watch the tumbler again. The water level does not go down. This activity shows that water is not seeping through the glass tumbler. However, it alone cannot prove that all the outside water comes only from condensation.

On a plant, you can see dew drops. You also see water drops gathering on the inner side of a steel plate covering boiling water. The change of water vapour into liquid water is called condensation.

You then visit an Atmospheric Water Generator machine. It collects water from humid air to produce drinkable water. Your tour ends with a new question: which clues show condensation, and which need more checking?

activities.title: A Tour of Water
activities.body:
Come with us on a journey through water. You will meet its three everyday states. Watch each one behave differently.

First, you find ice in the solid state. No matter the container, ice keeps its own shape. It cannot flow or spread.

Next, you see liquid water. It flows and changes its shape to fit its container. Yet its volume stays constant, even as its shape changes. When you heat ice, it melts. It becomes liquid water.

Melting changes a solid into a liquid. Freezing changes a liquid into a solid. Heating the liquid further changes it into gaseous water. Then, water enters its gaseous state.

Finally, you follow water vapour as it spreads throughout the available space. It moves into every part of that space. Your tour shows solid ice, flowing water, and spreading vapour.

activities.title: Water's Great Escape
activities.body:
You join a simple investigation and meet two containers of water. One holds water in a bottle cap. The other is a plate. Your task is to watch the water closely. You measure the time needed for each amount to evaporate completely.

The bottle cap has less exposed water area than the plate. Water spread on the plate has a larger area exposed to air. You change one condition while the other condition remains the same.

Because the exposed area is larger on the plate, its water evaporates faster. You notice that water evaporates faster from a cap kept in sunlight. You also see clothes drying faster on a hot, sunny day.

Now you test another condition by increasing the movement of air. The water evaporates faster when air moves more strongly. On a rainy day, water evaporates slowly. When the air has more humidity, water evaporates slowly. You see that several conditions affect how quickly water evaporates.

Sunlight and moving air also make it evaporate faster. Air with more humidity (water in the air) slows evaporation. Rainy days also slow evaporation. A fair test changes only one thing. It keeps the other things the same. It measures how long the water takes to evaporate completely.

activities.title: Handpicking and Threshing
activities.body:
You begin with handpicking. It means removing unwanted pieces from a mixture by hand. You look for particles that differ in size, colour and shape.

Handpicking is convenient when unwanted particles are few and easy to pick. It is useful when you can easily remove the unwanted pieces by hand.

Malli shows you whole black peppers. He picked them from the pulao with his fingers. This is handpicking because he uses his fingers.

Next, you visit harvested stalks spread in the sun to dry. Farmers then beat the stalks on a large wooden log. Beating stalks to separate their grains is called threshing. You watch the threshing separate grains from the stalks.

Many grains remain attached to each wheat stalk before threshing. After beating, the separated grains get mixed with piles of husk.

activities.title: Separating Grains and Flour
activities.body:
You arrive at a farm, ready to see how wheat is separated. A farmer shows you a bamboo tray, called a soop. The tray holds threshed wheat. He moves it in the direction of the wind.

As the air blows, heavier and lighter components become separated. You watch carefully as the moving air sorts the mixture. This separation by wind or blown air is called winnowing.

Next, you see a modern thresher. It separates grains from stalks and husk. A thresher performs threshing and winnowing at the same time. Modern technology has led to the development of these machines.

Afterwards, you see a sieve used to remove bran from flour. Fine flour particles pass through its holes. Bran and small stones remain on the sieve. You notice how the small flour travels, while larger pieces stay above.

Sieving is used for solid mixtures with components of different sizes. It separates solids according to differences in particle size. You finish your tour understanding three separation methods.

lessons.title: Decantation, Sedimentation and Filtration

activities.prompt: What will you discover about tea leaves, muddy water, and rice?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Tea, Mud and Pulses
activities.body:
Imagine a cup of tea, with tea leaves resting at the bottom of the vessel. You leave the tea undisturbed, giving the tea leaves time to settle. Now tilt the vessel and pour off the clear liquid. This removal of liquid by tilting is called decantation.

Pour the tea through a strainer, and the tea leaves separate from the tea. Decantation has not removed every tea leaf from it. Filter paper has very fine pores for trapping tiny particles. Cloth also has very small holes between its woven threads.

Picture muddy liquid passing through filter paper. The mud is left on the paper as a residue. The clear liquid that passes through your filter is called the filtrate.

Next, watch a heavier insoluble component settling in a liquid. This process is called sedimentation, and it takes place at the bottom. After the solid settles, tilt the vessel and decant the liquid. Decantation is also used to wash and clean rice and pulses.

activities.prompt: What wonders can you uncover through churning and magnetic separation?

activities.title: Churning and Magnetic Separation
activities.body:
You begin by watching curd being churned with a churner called a mathni. You watch until butter is obtained from the curd. You remember the tool's name and the process. You now know what churning produces.

Next, you meet sawdust containing iron nails. You watch a magnet attract all the nails. You learn that substances attracted towards a magnet are called magnetic substances. Iron is a common magnetic substance. That is why you see the iron nails moving towards the magnet.

Then you watch a magnetic separation demonstration. A magnet separates magnetic and non-magnetic substances. You compare the iron nails with the sawdust around them. You see the magnetic part move towards the magnet. You now understand how this separation works.

Finally, you visit a waste sorting place. Recyclers use magnets to separate iron articles from waste. You then see a crane-mounted magnet at work. It separates scrap iron from waste materials. You connect this scene with the sawdust demonstration. You now know why magnets help separate iron from waste.

Crane-mounted magnets separate scrap iron from waste materials.

lessons.title: What Makes the Living Apart from Non-living?

activities.prompt: How can you tell whether something is alive?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Living Things
activities.body:
You begin your tour by meeting a plant. Its flowers open, showing movement. It does not move from one place to another.

You watch living beings grow larger during their lives. They need food for their growth and development. Every living being respires. Breathing is part of this process, called respiration.

You also watch living beings remove waste from their bodies. This process is called excretion.

During your tour, you learn about stimuli. A stimulus is anything or any event that makes a living being respond. Plants also respond to stimuli. When you touch a touch-me-not plant, it folds its leaves.

You learn that reproduction produces new living beings of the same kind. A living being is dead when it cannot show all life characteristics. This remains true even when it has the needed resources. Anything without any life characteristics is classified as non-living.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Signs of Life
activities.body: Living beings show several signs of life. They grow bigger as they live. They need food. Respiration is the process that includes breathing. Excretion removes waste from the body. A stimulus is something that makes a living being respond. Reproduction makes new living beings of the same kind. Plants also respond. Their flowers open. Touch-me-not leaves fold when touched. A thing with none of these signs is non-living.
keyPoints: Living beings grow, need food, respire and remove waste.
They respond to stimuli and reproduce.
Plants can move parts but stay in one place.
A thing with no sign of life is non-living.
activities.explanation: These signs help you tell living beings from non-living things.

lessons.title: Essential Conditions for Germination of a Seed

activities.prompt: What does a seed need to turn into a little plant?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Starting a Seed
activities.body:
Imagine that you are holding a bean seed and wondering what it needs next. You place it in soil, but the seed is not a sprout yet. A seed has germinated when it turns into a sprout.

First, give it water. Seeds require water for germination. Water helps the seed carry out the processes needed for growth. It also softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo inside. You have learned why water matters.

Next, check the air around it. Seeds use the air found in the spaces between soil particles. These spaces also help roots grow easily. Bean seeds need the right amounts of both water and air to germinate.

Should you put the seed in sunlight? Light is not essential for bean seeds to germinate. Most seeds do not need light either. After germination, sunlight is needed for further growth. Some seeds, such as Coleus and Petunia, need light to germinate. Others, such as Calendula and Zinnia, need darkness. You can now check each seed’s needs before you plant it.

activities.title: What Does a Seed Need?
activities.body: A seed germinates when it turns into a sprout. Seeds need water and air. Water softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo. Seeds use air found in spaces between soil particles. These spaces also help roots grow easily. Most seeds do not need light to germinate. Sunlight helps further growth after germination. Some seeds, such as Coleus and Petunia, need light. Others, such as Calendula and Zinnia, need darkness.
keyPoints: Water softens the seed coat and helps the tiny embryo.
Seeds need air found between soil particles.
Most seeds do not need light to germinate.
activities.explanation: Water and air help a seed become a sprout.

lessons.title: Growth and Movement in Plants

activities.prompt: What helps a plant know which way to grow?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Plants Grow and Move
activities.body:
You begin with a germinated seed. It develops into a seedling with a small root and shoot. Now you visit three beakers, labelled A, B and C. In beaker A, a seedling stands upright. Wet blotting paper gives moisture to the seedling.

Next, you look at beaker B. The seedling in beaker B is inverted. Its shoot points downwards. Its root points upwards. The root bends and grows downwards. The shoot bends and grows upwards.

Then you visit beaker C. The seedling here receives light from only one direction. Its shoot grows towards the light. The root keeps growing downwards. You watch the shoot change its direction.

Finally, you compare the plants. In an upright plant, the root grows downwards and the shoot grows upwards. In an inverted plant, both parts bend towards their usual directions. With light from one side, the shoot grows towards it. Plant shoots grow upwards and show movement towards sunlight. You have watched growth and movement.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.body: A seed that has germinated (started to sprout) grows into a seedling. A seedling has a small root and shoot. In an upright plant, roots grow down and shoots grow up. If you turn a plant upside down, its parts bend. Each part grows in its normal direction. Roots bend down. Shoots bend up. When light comes from one side, the shoot grows towards it. The root keeps growing down.

Roots grow down and shoots grow up.
Shoots grow towards light from one side.
activities.explanation: Plants change how they grow, so they grow correctly.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Plant

activities.prompt: How does a tiny seed become the next generation of plants?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Bean’s Life Cycle
activities.body:
You begin your journey with a bean seed. It needs suitable conditions if it is to grow. Soon, you watch germination happen. A young plant appears, and you see leaves as it grows.

Next, you follow the plant towards its flowers. You can record how long the first flower takes to appear. This time belongs in your observation notes.

After flowering, you notice that some flower parts may dry. The plant may still grow further. Other parts of the flower can develop into a pod or fruit.

You look inside the bean plant’s fruit. It is a pod, and it holds seeds. The plant may also turn yellow and dry. This happens even when it continues to receive water.

Finally, you consider what happens next. The seeds can grow into a new generation of bean plants. Your journey from seed to plant and next seeds is a plant’s life cycle. A plant is considered dead when its growth and life activities gradually stop. This can happen even when necessary conditions remain available.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: A Plant's Life Cycle
activities.body: A bean plant starts as a seed. With the right conditions, it germinates and grows into a young plant. Germination means beginning to grow. The young plant grows leaves, flowers and fruit. Then the plant dies. Its flowers can dry up. Other flower parts can become a pod. A pod holds seeds. These seeds can grow into new bean plants. This whole journey is the plant's life cycle.

A pod has seeds for new plants.
The whole journey is the plant's life cycle.
activities.explanation: A seed starts the cycle, and new seeds continue it.

activities.prompt: How do mosquitoes and silk moths grow and change?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Life Journeys
activities.body:
Imagine you are taking a tour of two life cycles. First, you meet a female mosquito. She can spread diseases such as malaria, dengue and chikungunya.

You follow her to water, where she lays her eggs on or near it. The cycle continues. Next, you see a larva and a pupa. These are two different stages in mosquito development.

Both larvae and pupae live in water and need air for respiration. You watch them come to the water surface to get air. Then the pupa changes into an adult mosquito.

Now you tour the silk moth’s life cycle. It passes through the egg, larva, pupa and adult stages. During the larva stage, it makes a thread-like material. People use this material to make silk fabric.

Finally, you learn that mosquito breeding should be prevented. You should not allow water to stagnate around you. Kerosene oil forms a thin layer over the surface of water.

activities.body: Female mosquitoes can spread malaria, dengue and chikungunya. So, stop mosquitoes from breeding. Do not let water stay still around you. Mosquito larvae and pupae live in water. They need air. They come up to the surface to breathe. The pupa changes into an adult. The female lays eggs on or near water. Silk moths go through four stages: egg, larva, pupa and adult.

Silk moths pass through four stages.

lessons.title: Life Cycle of a Frog

activities.prompt: What might you discover while following a frog's life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Frog's Life Cycle
activities.body:
You begin your journey beside water, where you notice jelly-like eggs. These eggs are called spawn. You follow a frog through its four-stage life cycle.

First, you see the egg stage. It develops into the embryo stage. The early tadpole has a tail but no legs. Its tail helps it swim in water.

Next, you meet a later tadpole. It now has hind legs. Its tail still helps it swim in water. You notice that its habitat has changed.

Now, you follow the froglet. This stage comes between the tadpole and adult frog. You see it living in water. You also see it spending some time on land. Its habitat changes during this part of its life.

Finally, you watch the growing frog lose its tail completely. Its legs become strong enough for jumping and landing. The adult frog can live both in water and on land. Your journey ends as you watch the adult frog.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How a Frog Changes
activities.body: A frog goes through four life stages. Its jelly-like eggs are called spawn. Spawn grows into an embryo. A tadpole has a tail but no legs. Later, the tadpole grows hind legs (back legs). A froglet lives in water and on land. The growing frog loses its tail. Its strong legs help it jump. So an adult frog can live in water and on land.

The egg stage grows into the embryo stage.
A frog's habitat changes as it grows.
activities.explanation: You have followed the main changes in a frog's life.

lessons.title: Air and Wind

activities.prompt: What is wind, and how does it make windmills turn?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Air and Wind
activities.body:
Imagine taking a deep breath. Fresh air fills your lungs and helps you stay healthy. That air carries oxygen, which your body needs for its activities. Without it, you cannot live for even a few minutes without oxygen.

Now look around you. Air is a mixture of several gases. It contains nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. Percentage shows how many parts are in one hundred. You can use percentage to compare these parts of air.

Next, meet the moving part. Moving air is called wind. You see a firki spinning because the wind pushes its blades. Windmills can also draw water from wells. Some can generate electricity for people to use. Would you like to visit a place with many windmills?

A windmill farm contains many windmills. In India, Muppandal, Jaisalmer and Brahmanvel are among the leading windmill farms. Stand safely nearby and watch each firki rotate. You can now see how air, oxygen and wind work together.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Air, Breathing and Wind
activities.body: Air around the Earth is a mixture of gases. It has nitrogen, oxygen, argon, carbon dioxide and other gases. The air we breathe in has oxygen. Our body needs oxygen to do its work. Deep breaths bring more fresh air into your lungs. This helps us stay healthy. Moving air is called wind. Wind makes a firki turn. Windmills can draw water from wells and make electricity.
keyPoints: Air has several gases, including oxygen.
Our body needs oxygen to do its work.
Moving air is called wind.
Wind can help useful machines work.
activities.explanation: These facts connect breathing, gases, wind and windmill uses.

lessons.title: Water and Its Careful Use

activities.prompt: How can your family use water wisely every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Water
activities.body:
Imagine starting your day with a glass of water. You need it for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and cleaning.

You also see water helping plants grow. Farmers use it for crops, and industries use it too. From above, water covers about two-thirds of the Earth’s surface. Most of it lies in oceans and seas. This ocean water is saline, which means it is salty.

Visit freshwater places. You find it as ice, snow, rivers, lakes and underground water. Only a small part of this freshwater is easily accessible.

At home, care for every drop. Turning off taps and repairing leaks can reduce water wastage.

Polluted water cannot be consumed by living beings. Many parts of India face water shortages because freshwater sources are limited. Rainwater harvesting collects and stores rainwater for later use. You can help by saving water and harvesting rainwater.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Why Water Matters
activities.body: Water is needed for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing and cleaning. It also helps grow crops and supports industries. Most Earth's water lies in oceans and seas. This salt water is not the easily accessible freshwater we use. Only a small part of freshwater is easily accessible. Careful use and rainwater harvesting can help us.
keyPoints: Water has many everyday uses.
Most water is salty ocean water.
Only a small part of freshwater is easily accessible.
activities.explanation: Water is useful, but easy freshwater is limited.

activities.explanation: Ocean water is saline, which means it is salty.

activities.title: Protecting Our Water
activities.body: Most water on Earth is in oceans and seas. This water is salty. Fresh water is in ice, snow, rivers, lakes, and under the ground. Only a small part is easy to use. Polluted water is dirty. We cannot drink it. Turning off taps and fixing leaks saves water. Rainwater harvesting means saving rain for later.

Leaks and running taps waste water.
Rainwater can be collected and saved.
activities.explanation: Careful habits help us keep fresh water safe.

lessons.title: Energy from the Sun and Forests

activities.prompt: How does sunlight help forests grow and power your home?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Sunlight and Forest Life
activities.body:
Begin your visit in a forest. You look around a large area and see many kinds of plants growing close together. The Sun is the main source of energy on Earth. This forest is a natural home for wild animals, birds and insects.

Now follow the sunlight to the leaves. Plants use it to prepare their food. Grass also needs sunlight to grow. All plants and animals here depend on the Sun.

Next, imagine an animal taking a bite of grass. It gains energy by eating plants, and that energy helps it grow. This is a simple journey of energy through the forest.

Now step towards a house. Solar panels capture the Sun's energy and make electricity. In another place, sunlight can be used directly for cooking. We use the Sun's heat and light in many ways.

Finally, remember what happens when too many trees are cut down. Large-scale cutting has reduced forest cover. A new forest takes many years to grow. Restoring a lost forest also takes many years.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Sun Power and Forest Life
activities.body: The Sun is the main energy source for Earth. Its heat and light help us and living things. Sunlight helps plants make food. Grass needs sunlight to grow. Animals get energy by eating plants. Solar panels catch sunlight and make electricity. Forests have many plants. Forests give homes to wild animals, birds and insects. Cutting trees makes the forest cover smaller. Growing back a forest takes many years.
keyPoints: The Sun is Earth's main energy source.
Plants need sunlight. Animals get energy from eating plants.
Forests give homes to wildlife. Cutting trees makes forest cover smaller.
activities.explanation: The Sun gives power to living things. Forests give homes to wild animals.

lessons.title: Soil, Rocks and Minerals

activities.prompt: What wonders hide beneath your feet, and how were they made?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Soil and Rocks
activities.body:
You begin your journey in a forest. You lift a fallen leaf and look at the soil. Around you, the forest contains different types of soil.

Earthworms wriggle through the ground. They help turn and loosen the soil. Spaces between soil particles hold air. They also give roots room to grow. Fallen leaves decay and add nutrients to the soil.

Here, your guide explains that soil forms slowly. Rocks break apart over a long time. The Sun, water and living organisms help this process. Even rocks take thousands to millions of years to form.

You then visit a rocky hillside. Each rock is made up of minerals. Important metals can be obtained from minerals. Rocks are useful. People use them to build houses, roads, dams and other structures.

Finally, you think about protecting nature's treasures. Soil supports biodiversity. That makes soil precious. We must conserve and use rocks responsibly. Your tour ends, but your care can continue.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: How Soil Helps Living Things
activities.body: Rocks break into small bits over a long time. The Sun, water and living things break rocks. This is how soil is made. Spaces between soil bits give air and room for roots. Earthworms help turn and loosen soil. Fallen leaves decay (break down) and add nutrients (food) to soil. Soil helps biodiversity. Biodiversity means the variety of living things.
keyPoints: Soil forms as rocks break into small bits.
Earthworms and fallen leaves help soil.
Spaces between soil bits give air and room for roots.
activities.explanation: Soil helps many living things. It is very valuable.

activities.explanation: Spaces between soil particles provide air and room for roots.

activities.explanation: Earthworms work the soil and make it looser.

activities.explanation: Decaying leaves return nutrients to the soil.

activities.prompt: Why is soil a precious treasure?
options: It supports biodiversity.
It is used to build dams.

It forms houses and roads.
activities.explanation: Soil supports biodiversity, which means the variety of living things.

activities.title: Rocks and Their Uses
activities.body: Rocks are used to build houses, roads, dams and other structures. Minerals make up rocks, and important metals come from minerals. Rocks take thousands to millions of years to form. We must conserve and use them responsibly. Forests contain different types of soils.
keyPoints: Rocks have many uses in building.
Minerals make up rocks.
Rocks need careful, responsible use.
activities.explanation: Rocks are useful, but they take a very long time to form.

lessons.title: Fossil Fuels

activities.prompt: What might you discover underground during a journey through fossil fuels?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Journey Through Fossil Fuels
activities.body:
Imagine you begin a journey underground, following fuels that power our daily lives. First, you meet petroleum, from which we obtain petrol, diesel and kerosene. These fuels, together with natural gas and coal, are called fossil fuels.

Next, you travel back through time as plants and tiny organisms are buried. You wait millions of years while their buried remains slowly form fossil fuels.

You learn that the most widely used vehicle fuels are petrol and diesel.

You visit a kitchen, where natural gas helps cook food. At a power station, you see coal used mainly to produce electricity. You also see natural gas used to generate electricity. Natural gas is cleaner than petrol or diesel.

Outside, you watch smoke and carbon dioxide rise as fossil fuels burn. They pollute the air when we use too much fossil fuel for transport and cooking. Finally, you walk or cycle to a nearby place and conserve fossil fuels. Remember, these fuels are available only in limited quantities.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: What are fossil fuels?
activities.body: Petroleum, natural gas, and coal are fossil fuels. They form from the buried remains of plants and tiny organisms. This process takes millions of years. Fossil fuels are available only in limited quantities. Burning them releases smoke and carbon dioxide, which pollute the air. Walking or cycling nearby helps conserve fossil fuels.

Fossil fuels take millions of years to form.
Burning fossil fuels can pollute the air.

lessons.title: Renewable and Non-renewable Resources

activities.prompt: How can we use natural resources in a caring way?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour of Natural Resources
activities.body:
You begin a journey through a forest beside flowing water and under the bright Sun. Nature supplies natural resources. People also make human-made resources to meet their needs.

As you walk, you see air, water and forests around you. These renewable natural resources can be renewed or restored within a reasonable time. The Sun’s energy is also an important natural resource.

Then you visit a place filled with soil, rocks and minerals. These resources do not get replenished within a reasonable time. They are non-renewable resources. Coal, petroleum and natural gas are also non-renewable.

Your tour shows how important natural resources are. You use air, water, soil, and food from plants and animals every day. Careful use today can meet our present needs while saving resources for the future.

Outside, you notice vehicles passing through the city. Smoke from vehicles can make city air polluted. Electric vehicles do not release smoke. You can help by conserving natural resources and using them responsibly.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Kinds of natural resources
activities.body: Natural resources come from nature. People also make human-made resources to meet their needs. Renewable resources come back again in a reasonable time. Air, water and forests are renewable natural resources. Minerals, soil, rocks, coal, petroleum and natural gas are non-renewable resources. We must save natural resources. We must use them well for the future.
keyPoints: Renewable resources come back within a reasonable time.
Air, water and forests are renewable natural resources.
Coal and petroleum are non-renewable resources.
activities.explanation: This helps you know the difference between natural, renewable and non-renewable resources.

activities.title: A Tour of Nubra's Night Sky
activities.body:
You arrive in Nubra, a beautiful region in Ladakh. Yangdol and her twin brother Dorjay live in a village here. They invite you to leave the village after dark and look up.

The night sky is almost cloudless. Thousands of stars light up the whole night. Nubra has very little air or light pollution. So you can see the stars clearly.

Each star produces its own light. As your eyes travel across the sky, groups of stars seem to form patterns. These patterns are called constellations.

Ancient people connected these patterns with animals, things and characters from stories. You might recognise figures that helped them imagine the night sky. Recognising them was useful for finding directions.

Long ago, sailors and travellers used star patterns to find their way. You try their method by turning towards a familiar pattern. There are 88 officially listed constellations, and together they divide the entire sky. Under Nubra's open sky, you see why such patterns mattered.

activities.title: A Tour of the Night Sky
activities.body:
You step outside on a clear, cloudless night, ready to explore the sky. Many stars may greet you, but some places hide them well. Smoke, dust and bright lights can hide many stars. Excessive artificial light at night is called light pollution.

Light pollution is growing quickly around the world. Tall buildings and trees may block your view of the sky. The best place for night-sky watching is an open, dark area. Ask an adult to help you choose a dark, open place. Never go to a dark open place at night without an adult.

Once you are safely there, wait about half an hour. Your eyes adjust to the darkness during that time. You can download a sky-mapping app on a mobile phone.

You cannot see every constellation from every place on Earth. Your place on Earth affects which constellations you can see.

Now you are ready to explore the stars with your app. You have planned a safe visit to a dark, open place.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.body: On a clear, cloudless night, many stars may be visible. Smoke, dust and light pollution can hide many stars. Light pollution means excessive artificial light at night. It is growing quickly. We cannot see every constellation from every place on Earth. Tall buildings and trees may block the view. The best place is open and dark. Ask an adult. Never go alone. Wait about half an hour so your eyes adjust.
keyPoints: Clear, cloudless nights may show many stars.
Light pollution can hide stars and is growing quickly.
Choose a dark, open place with an adult.
Wait about half an hour so your eyes adjust.

activities.prompt: What will you discover about the Sun and our solar system?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Around the Sun
activities.body:
Imagine beginning a journey from the Sun towards Earth. You might first wonder what this glowing centre really is. The Sun is a star, and it is the closest star to us. During your journey, you discover that it gives Earth heat and light. It is also Earth's main source of energy. The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth.

From here, you look back and imagine the huge space between you and the Sun. It is about 150 million kilometres away. One astronomical unit is about the distance between the Sun and Earth. Proxima Centauri is about 269000 astronomical units away.

Now you watch a planet moving around the Sun. This movement is called revolution. A planet is a large, nearly spherical object that revolves around the Sun. Earth is one such planet, taking nearly one year to complete one revolution.

Your tour shows that Earth is also rotating about its axis.
activities.explanation: Reading first helps the ideas stick.

activities.title: Our Bright Neighbour
activities.body: The Sun is a star and the closest star to us. It gives Earth heat and light. It is Earth's main energy source. The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth. Earth is about 150 million kilometres from it. One astronomical unit means the Sun-to-Earth distance. Revolution means an object's movement around the Sun. Earth also rotates about its axis. This means Earth spins around its axis.

The Sun gives Earth heat and light.
Revolution means movement around the Sun.

activities.prompt: How do planets, moons and craters differ?

activities.title: A Tour Through Space
activities.body:
You begin among the eight planets. You meet Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

First, you visit the smaller inner planets. They are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. You find that their solid surfaces are covered with rocks. Then, you look towards the four outermost planets. You see that they are much larger than Earth. They are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.

Venus catches your eye as it shines brightly at dawn and dusk. You learn that it is called the Morning Star or Evening Star. Yet, Venus is not a star.

Mars looks red as you watch it, so it is called the Red Planet. Earth looks blue because much of it is covered with water. You call it the Blue Planet.

Now, you discover moons, which are natural satellites of planets. Earth has one Moon, while Mars has two moons. You watch the Moon take about 27 days to revolve around Earth. On its surface, you see round, bowl-shaped hollows called craters.

activities.title: Space Neighbours
activities.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are the inner planets. They are smaller, with rocky surfaces. The four outer planets are much larger than Earth. Venus shines at dawn and dusk, but it is not a star. Mars looks red. Earth is called the Blue Planet. Moons are natural satellites that travel around planets. The Moon takes about 27 days to circle Earth. Its bowl-shaped hollows are called craters.
keyPoints: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are smaller inner planets with rocky surfaces.
The four outer planets are much larger than Earth.
Moons travel around planets, and craters are bowl-shaped hollows.

activities.prompt: How does a comet change as it travels near the Sun?

activities.title: Asteroids and Comets
activities.body:
Imagine you are visiting the region between Mars and Jupiter. You meet small rocky objects travelling around the Sun. These small rocky objects are called asteroids. Many asteroids travel around the Sun here. This region is called the asteroid belt.

Next, you spot a visitor with a long tail. This is a comet. Comets are made of dust, gases, rocks and ice. Their frozen material starts evaporating when they near the Sun. You follow this icy-rocky visitor on its journey.

During your journey, you watch the comet move away from the Sun. It becomes dim as the distance grows. You still see its long tail. You remember what the comet contains. Dust, gases, rocks and ice make up its mixture. Near the Sun, its frozen material starts evaporating.

Scientists understand comets as icy-rocky visitors travelling near the Sun. You have met one during your tour. You have also seen many rocky asteroids. They travel around the Sun between Mars and Jupiter. This region is called the asteroid belt.

They are made of dust, gases, rocks and ice. Frozen material in a comet starts evaporating when it nears the Sun. A comet becomes dim as it moves away from the Sun. Scientists understand comets as icy-rocky visitors travelling near the Sun.

lessons.title: The Milky Way Galaxy and the Universe

activities.prompt: What is the Milky Way, and could we find life elsewhere?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Tour Beyond Our Galaxy
activities.body:
Imagine you stand in a dark place on a moonless night. You look upward and notice a faint band of light across the sky. The band stretches from near north to south.

Your home galaxy is called the Milky Way Galaxy, or Ākāśha Gangā. Our Solar System is part of it. A galaxy can contain millions to billions of stars.

Now picture yourself visiting other galaxies. Scientists study galaxies to understand stars, galaxies, and the Universe. You might ask whether planets revolve around other stars in our galaxy. Such planets are called exoplanets.

Here is a careful answer to a big question. We do not yet know whether life exists elsewhere in the Universe. Scientists have not yet found any evidence of life elsewhere. Your question remains open, so keep following your curiosity.

End your tour by looking up once more. You now know our Solar System is part of the Milky Way Galaxy. You have learned that exoplanets revolve around other stars in our galaxy. What will you explore next?

activities.body: Look at the sky on a dark night with no moon. You can see a faint (weak) band of light. The band goes from near north to south across the sky. This band is our home galaxy. It is called the Milky Way Galaxy. It is also called Ākāśha Gangā. A galaxy can have millions to billions of stars. Our Solar System is part of it.
